The `users` and `permissions` TABLES are untouched and keep their rows; dropping them is a migration, and a separate decision.

**AND THE NAMES.** `routes/purchases.js` is now a library sitting in the routes folder, and `restock`, `push` and `ai` still carry kitchen-era names. Renaming is cosmetic, touches load order that `routes/retail-purchasing.js`'s header calls out explicitly, and is deliberately NOT bundled into a diff this size.

## §82 — TIME IS A TENANT PROPERTY, NEVER A HOST PROPERTY

Ruling (Ash, 2026-09-09), following the delivery-logic survey
(`docs/surveys/delivery-logic-survey.md`, finding F2), which found the entire
delivery calendar computing in host-local time while the repository asserted
the production offset three times and contradicted itself once.

**EVERY DATE AND TIME DECISION IS EVALUATED IN THE TENANT'S TIMEZONE.** Delivery
cutoffs, batch dates, slot generation, business-date rollover, "today",
"tomorrow", pre-order gates — all of it resolves in the timezone of the tenant
that owns the order, read from a tenant setting.

**NO BUSINESS DECISION MAY READ THE HOST CLOCK'S LOCAL TIME.**
`new Date().getHours()`, `.getFullYear()`, `.getDate()`, `.toDateString()` and
their equivalents are **forbidden anywhere a cutoff, a date or a slot is
computed.** The host offset is an accident of deployment. It is not a business
fact and may not be read as one.

**THE PRODUCTION HOST IS PINNED TO UTC, DELIBERATELY, AND THE DEPLOY CONFIG MUST
SET IT EXPLICITLY.** This is not neutrality for its own sake: it is so that any
code still reading host-local time is **visibly wrong rather than silently
correct for one tenant.** A host that happened to run UTC+8 would make every
un-migrated call site produce right answers for Roots and wrong ones for
everybody else, which is the failure that hides. **A tenant timezone that
happens to match the host is a coincidence, not a fallback.**

**ROOTS IS `Asia/Shanghai` (UTC+8). OTHER TENANTS WILL BE ELSEWHERE.** The
offset is per tenant, not per platform.

**A TENANT WITH NO TIMEZONE SET IS A CONFIGURATION ERROR AND MUST FAIL LOUDLY AT
STARTUP.** It does not default. A default here is the same mistake as a host
fallback wearing different clothes — it produces a working system that is
quietly wrong for whoever was not thought about.

**CI RUNS WITH THE HOST IN UTC**, so timezone-dependent logic cannot pass tests
by inheriting a convenient offset. `.github/workflows/tests.yml` currently pins
`TZ: Asia/Shanghai` for the opposite reason — its comment says production runs
UTC+8 — and that pin is what made F2 invisible to the suite. It goes.

**WHAT THIS RULING DOES NOT DO.** It does not migrate the call sites. The survey
lists them (`routes/retail.js` — `parseYmdLocal` / `toYmdLocal`,
`earliestBatchMakeDate`, `nextFreshBatchDate`, `computeDeliverySlots`,
`expressEarliestIso`, `rescheduleEligibility`); `lib/business-date.js` already
does the right thing per location and is the shape to copy. That work is its own
change and is not started.

## §83 — EVERY DISTRICT MUST BE COVERED; AN UNMATCHED ADDRESS IS REFUSED

Ruling (Ash, 2026-09-09), following the delivery-logic survey
(`docs/surveys/delivery-logic-survey.md`, findings F1 and F23), which found
`/checkout/quote` refusing an unmatched address while `POST /orders` accepted it
and priced it on a legacy flat fee.

**A TENANT'S DELIVERY ZONE TABLE MUST COVER EVERY DISTRICT IT SERVES.** Coverage
is a **data obligation on the tenant**, enforced by the platform. It is not
something the code works around.

**AN ADDRESS MATCHING NO ZONE IS A CONFIGURATION ERROR, NOT A DELIVERY OPTION.**
Every path that can create an order refuses it, with an explicit error, and
**identically** — the refusal does not vary by entry point.

**THERE IS NO LEGACY FEE FALLBACK, NO DEFAULT FEE, AND NO DEFAULT SLOT SET FOR AN
UNMATCHED ADDRESS.** A guessed fee is worse than a refusal, because **a refusal
is visible and a wrong fee is not.** The order is created, the customer is
charged a number nobody configured, and nothing anywhere reports it.

**THE RULE `/checkout/quote` ALREADY APPLIES IS THE CORRECT ONE.** All other
order-creation paths conform to it. It is **not** relaxed to match them — which
is the direction the code drifted, and the direction that looks like
compatibility while being a silent loss of control.

**WHAT THIS RULING DOES NOT DO.** It does not ship the refusal. Filling the
coverage gap comes first: a district that has taken real orders and is missing
from `retail_delivery_zones` would start rejecting them the day the refusal
lands. The zone-coverage report is the gate on that work, and the survey's F23
records why an unmatched Guangzhou district reaches this path at all
(`matchDeliveryZone` returns null rather than falling through once any
`gz_district` row exists).

### §83 addendum — the refusal is the CUSTOMER's; staff are not blocked (2026-09-09)

§83 above says an address matching no zone is refused by "every path that can create an
order". Read literally that includes the operator keying an order in by hand, and it
should not.

**The two rules only appear to conflict.** §83's reason is stated in its own text: *a
guessed fee is worse than a refusal, because a refusal is visible and a wrong fee is not.*
The harm it names is a fee **nobody chose** being charged silently. On the staff path
there is no such fee — `POST /api/retail-admin/orders` never matched a zone in the first
place; the operator types the shipping fee. `manualOrderFees` is a *quote* that prefills
two fields, and the create route never consults it. So §83's harm cannot occur there, and
refusing would cost something real: a shop on the phone to a customer in a district
nobody has configured yet would have to turn the order away.

`lib/…`/`routes/retail.js`'s `manualOrderFees` already carried that rule before §83 was
written — *"An address in a district nobody has configured refuses the CUSTOMER (they
can't be charged a fee that doesn't exist), but it must never refuse STAFF: the shop still
takes the order and someone works the zone out later."* **That rule stands. §83 does not
override it, and did not intend to.**

**What §83 DOES change on the staff path:** the operator is told *which* place has no
zone. `manualOrderFees` returns `unmatched` beside its `no_zone_match`, so the error names
the province/city/district to add rather than handing back a bare code and leaving the
reader to work it out.

**Pinned by a test, not by this paragraph.** `scripts/test_manual_order_fees.js` asserts
the non-refusal directly — the quote comes back with zero fees, no refusal flag, and the
order stays keyable — so a later reading of §83 that tries to make the staff path refuse
turns that assertion red before it reaches production.

**Not delegated, and reversible.** Ash asked for the question to be settled rather than
left open; this is the answer, with the reasoning above rather than an appeal to the older
comment. If the intent is that staff should also be blocked, that is a one-line change and
the test that pins the current behaviour is the one to invert.

## §84 — THE SHELF TELLS THE TRUTH, AND WHAT IT OWES IS WHAT THE KITCHEN MAKES

**Decided by Ash, 2026-09-09**, in the session that asked how the §74/§80 pre-order rule reaches
Meituan, Eleme and gzgrocery. It does not reach them yet, and this section is the half that has to
exist before it can. **The pre-order window on the channels is NOT decided here** — it is named at
the end as the work this unblocks, so that a later reader does not mistake the prerequisite for the
feature.

### THE QUESTION THAT EXPOSED THE GAP

§80 made a sold-out fresh meal orderable in the mini app while today's batch is still coming. Ash
asked for the same on the three platforms. Walking the path back from the platform to the kitchen
found the rule cannot work there, and the reason is not the push:

> *"in the morning when kitchen come to work they already see how many fresh meals and wraps need to
> be prepared and they will add those extra to the batch they are about to do"*

**That is the right design and it is not what the system does.** Three findings, one cause:

1. **The kitchen's morning list never reads customer orders.** `retail_order_items` appears nowhere
   in `routes/restock.js`, `routes/retail-production.js` or `lib/kitchen-ready.js`. 厨房制作队列
   renders REQUESTS somebody typed. A night of orders with no request raised leaves the kitchen
   opening an empty queue.
2. **The waiting-orders card counts orders, not units, and excludes every platform** —
   `COALESCE(o.channel,'') NOT IN ('meituan','eleme','gzgrocery')`, as "read-only channel mirrors".
3. **A platform order on an empty shelf leaves no trace of what it owes.** The ingest clamps at zero
   and writes the shortfall to a JSON log column, in a table the same file describes as having "no
   index, no screen and nothing watching it".

**So the number the kitchen would add to its batch exists nowhere.** Not as a total, not per product,
not for any channel — the mini app included.

### THE RULING: THE NUMBER IS DERIVED, NEVER TYPED

**Ash chose automatic** when the fork was put to him: the morning number is computed from the orders
themselves, not raised as a request by a person reading a screen. The manual request path stays for
everything the orders do not cover; it is no longer the only way the kitchen learns what to make.

**AND THE NUMBER IS NOT A NEW CONCEPT — §39 ALREADY DEFINED IT.** `adjustStock` stopped flooring at
zero for exactly this reason, in words this section only has to point at:

> *"Negative one is ugly but true: it says stock was sold that was never held, which really
> happened."*

A platform order taken at 08:00 against an empty shelf **is** stock sold that was never held. The
shelf going to −18 is not a fault to be suppressed; it is the sentence "eighteen are owed", already
in the vocabulary this codebase decided on. So:

> **owed(store, product) = the distance the shelf has fallen below zero, plus the units on
> `awaiting_restock` orders — which hold no stock by design and so never dent the shelf at all.**

No new table, no forecast, no batch plan declared in advance, and nothing parsed out of a log.

### WHAT THIS MAKES TRUE, AND IT IS THE POINT

`adjustStock`'s own comment names the four channel-ingest paths that still compute
`Math.max(0, …)` and pass an absolute figure as **"recorded debt, per-channel work."** This section
pays off **the Meituan and Eleme half of it — four call sites, not two**: each channel clamps once
when an order arrives and again when a cancelled order comes back to life and is re-deducted, and a
debt lost on the second path is lost exactly as completely as one lost on the first. Unclamped, the
shelf carries the debt, the kitchen reads it, and the oversell alarm stops being the only record of
it. Eleme's own comment already said so — *"the shortfall vanishes into a Δ0 row unless it is
recorded here"* — and this is that shortfall being recorded where it belongs instead.

**GZGROCERY IS DELIBERATELY LEFT CLAMPED, AND IT IS NOT AN OMISSION.** It has no order-ingest path
to unclamp: gzgrocery sells through the Guanyi ERP and we never receive its order lines, so a sale
reaches us as an OBSERVED DROP in the ERP's own stock, reconciled by an operator through
`/guanyi/pickups/:id/apply`. That number is INFERRED, and the row it comes from is already flagged
`capped`. A debt derived from a real order line is a fact; a debt derived from an inference that
overshot is a phantom the kitchen would cook for. **The two are not the same fact and must not share
a mechanism** — which is also why gzgrocery's owed units simply do not arise: an ERP drop we
reconcile is a sale that already happened, not a promise waiting on a batch.

**THE TRUTH GOES NEGATIVE; THE NUMBER WE PUBLISH DOES NOT.** `bundle-stock.rawStockAt` returns the
raw column and `sellableAt` passes it straight through for a non-bundle, so an unclamped shelf would
push a NEGATIVE quantity to Meituan, Eleme and Guanyi. The floor belongs at the publish boundary and
nowhere else: our ledger is allowed to say −18 because it is true, and a platform is told 0 because
a platform cannot hold a debt. Clamping at the ingest — where it sits today — puts the floor on the
wrong side of the fact and is what destroys it.

### HOW IT RETURNS TO A TRUE NUMBER, AND THE DOOR THAT WOULD ERASE IT

Asked directly by Ash: *"after it's minus eighteen, how it will go back to the right stock?"*

**It corrects itself through the door the kitchen already uses.** 加库存 and Log a batch both pass
`deltaQty` — an increment, not a total (`routes/retail-inventory.js`, `routes/retail-production.js`).
−18 plus a batch of 40 is 22: the eighteen go to the people waiting and twenty-two stay on the shelf,
with no reset step and nothing to clean up. Ash's standing instruction to the kitchen — *做好一批,
马上加库存* — is already exactly this door.

**THE RECOUNT DOOR IS THE ONE THAT WOULD ERASE IT.** "Set the new total" writes an absolute
`newPhysicalQty`. Somebody standing at −18, seeing an empty shelf and typing 0, wipes the record that
eighteen are owed — and §46 deliberately asks nothing of an UPWARD correction, so it would happen in
silence. **A recount that raises the count across zero from a negative shelf must therefore
acknowledge what it is clearing**, on the model of the reason §46 already demands when lowering one.
The asymmetry §46 relies on — that raising a count is overwhelmingly a miscount being fixed — does
not hold once a negative can mean a debt.

### WHERE THE NUMBER IS SHOWN

**厨房制作队列 (`kitchenqueue`), above the request list, and it renders on an EMPTY queue** — that is
the case it exists for. One line per product, a name and a number, no buttons and no status: it is a
total, not a task with a state. The request list underneath is unchanged.

**Plus one row on the phone Home**, beside 厨房已完成, so it is seen before anything is opened. The
kitchen is not shown which channel a unit came from; they are shown how many to make.

Deliberately NOT on 加库存 (the wrong moment — the batch is already cooked), NOT on 登记批次 (that
records what was made), and NOT in the desktop back office, which §81's realm retirement is the long
record of the kitchen having no login for.

### WHAT IS NOT DECIDED HERE

**The pre-order window on Meituan, Eleme and gzgrocery is the next section's, not this one's.** Ash
has settled two of its parameters already — a lock hour defaulting to 11:00 **and adjustable**, and
all three channels in scope, gzgrocery included over this session's caution (*"I have no problem with
gzgrocery sync it works great"*) — but publishing a forward quantity to a platform is a separate
change with its own guard rails, and it is unsafe until the number above is visible to the kitchen.
This section makes the demand legible. It does not yet make it sellable.

## §85 — THE PRE-ORDER WINDOW REACHES THE PLATFORMS

**Decided by Ash, 2026-09-09**, and it is the half §84 deliberately did not build. §74 and §80 made a
sold-out fresh meal orderable in the mini app while today's batch is still coming; §84 made what is
owed visible to the kitchen. This carries the same morning to Meituan, Eleme and gzgrocery.

**TWO PARAMETERS WERE SET BY ASH AND ARE NOT THIS SECTION'S TO CHOOSE**: a lock hour defaulting to
**11:00 and adjustable** (*"let's say lock time is 11 am but it's need to be able to adjust"*), and
**all three channels in scope**, gzgrocery included over this session's caution about its silent
month of failed pushes (*"I have no problem with gzgrocery sync it works great"*).

### WHY THE MINI APP'S MECHANISM CANNOT BE COPIED

In the mini app the rule works by DECLINING TO REFUSE: `freshLinesCoveredToday` marks the line
covered, the five-option modal never opens, and the order parks holding no stock. **We own that
checkout.** On the three platforms we own nothing but a number we push — and every one of them
pushes the same one, `bundleStock.sellableAt`, through `lib/meituan-bundles.js`, `lib/eleme-sync.js`
and `lib/guanyi-sync.js`. A shelf at zero is pushed as zero and the listing reads 售罄. There is no
parking on a platform: an order it accepts is live, and an order we cannot fill is a cancellation
with a penalty attached.

**So the only way to make it orderable is to publish a number for food that does not exist yet**,
and everything below is the guard rails on doing that.

### THE RULE, IN ONE LINE

> **While the window is open: `published = max(0, shelf + preorder_qty)`. Otherwise: `max(0, shelf)`,
> which is exactly today's behaviour.**

The window is open when the schedule is enabled, today is a batch day, the hour is before
`lock_hour`, `preorder_qty` is set, and this channel is named. **Any one of those missing is the off
switch**, and with none of them set every tenant behaves precisely as it does today — the same shape
§74 chose for `ready_hour`, for the same reason: no migration, no backfill, nothing to undo.

**IT CAPS ITSELF, AND THAT IS WHY IT IS ONE TERM RATHER THAN A QUOTA MECHANISM.** Each pre-order
drives the shelf down by one (§84 having stopped the ingests clamping), so the published figure
falls by one with it. A `preorder_qty` of 20 against an empty shelf publishes 20, then 19, then 18;
at −20 it publishes 0 and the platform shows sold out. **The morning cannot sell more than the
allowance, and nothing has to remember how many it has sold** — the shelf already knows, because
§84 made it able to say so.

### ONE NUMBER FOR EVERY PRODUCT, AND IT IS DELIBERATE FOR NOW

`preorder_qty` is tenant-wide, on the Fresh batches card beside the hours. **A per-product allowance
is the obviously better answer and is NOT built here**, because it needs an editor the stock-layer
fields do not have — `safety_buffer`, `wechat_quota`, `meituan_quota` and `restock_target` are all
API-only today, with no control anywhere in the back office — and shipping a per-product number
nobody can set is worse than shipping a blunt one they can. **Recorded as the first thing to
revisit** once the kitchen has used it and can say whether one number fits every fresh line.

The same caution §74 attached to `ready_hour` applies with more force here and is restated rather
than assumed: **set `preorder_qty` only where the batch reliably covers it.** On the mini app a
surplus parks and waits; on a platform it is a cancellation.

### WHERE THE CADENCE LIVES, WHICH §84 LEFT OPEN

The window needs to know whether today is a batch day. That arithmetic lived in `routes/retail.js`
and a daemon cannot require it — requiring a 36,000-line express router to answer a date question is
not a dependency a stock daemon should carry. **`nextBatchShipDate` MOVES to `lib/batch-cadence.js`
and `routes/retail.js` calls it there.** It is a move, not a copy: §80 collapsed three copies of this
rule into one on the explicit ground that "the pill, the checkout and the order agree", and a fourth
copy in a daemon would undo exactly that. `lib/inventory.js` still learns nothing — §80's line holds,
and the suite that pins it is unchanged.

### THE CLOSE IS EXACT, NOT SWEPT

At `lock_hour` the published figure must fall back to the shelf **whether or not the batch was
recorded**, or a kitchen running forty minutes late leaves a platform selling food that does not
exist. The push queue is edge-triggered and nothing happens at 11:00 to trigger it.

The drift sweep would eventually catch it — it is the level-triggered backstop for exactly this —
but it runs every 30 minutes, and half an hour of selling past a lock the operator set to a
particular hour makes the setting a lie. **The daemons' own main loops run every ten seconds**, so
the flip is detected there: a config read and a comparison against the last-seen state, with no
browser, no network and no query when nothing has changed. The drift sweep remains the backstop it
already was.

### THE OVERSELL ALARM LEARNS THE DIFFERENCE

A pre-order taken against an empty shelf trips `order_oversold` today, which is correct in every
other circumstance and noise in this one. **An alert that fires on every pre-order buries the one
that matters**, and the alarm exists because 54 undeducted lines once accumulated unseen from June to
September. So the alert is suppressed exactly where the window explains it — the channel is in the
window and the shortfall is inside the allowance — and fires unchanged everywhere else, including
for a shortfall that exceeds the allowance, which is a real oversell wearing a pre-order's clothes.
**The sync-log row is still written in both cases.** Suppressing the page is not the same as
forgetting, and the log is where the count gets reconciled.

### WHAT IS STILL NOT SOLVED, NAMED SO IT IS NOT READ AS DONE

**The order that arrives one minute after the lock.** The kitchen has closed the batch; the platform
order is live and must be filled or cancelled. Narrowing the window shrinks that gap and never
closes it. §84's answer stands — this is the difference between a surface we own and one we do not,
and it is the cost of being sellable there at all.

## §86 — THE KITCHEN RAISES A PURCHASE REQUEST; THE BUYER TURNS IT INTO A DRAFT PO, AND THE MONEY STAYS THE BUYER'S

Ruling (Ash, 2026-09-09), on being asked how far "automatically" reaches: *"B"*, of the
two readings put to him — the request WAITS in Purchasing and the buyer converts it in one
action, rather than the send creating a PO outright. Two further answers in the same
message settle the unit and the holder: **the quantity is in the material's own configured
buy unit**, and **the kitchen role holds the new grant**.

### The finding this rests on, and it is most of the work

**THE BUYING END ALREADY EXISTS AND NEEDS NOTHING.** §77 recorded that kitchen purchasing
had already moved to Tacet in ordinary use — `RPO-0031`, eleven material lines, Ordered,
¥2,750, against Tianhe — on the `ingredient_id` line subject §28 addendum point 4 gave a
retail PO in Phase 1b. A material line already prices back into
`ingredient_price_history`, already fires the ±5% alert, already posts its expense, and
already refuses to touch `inventory.adjustStock`. **Nothing about the destination is
built here.**

**AND THE BRIDGE ALREADY EXISTS, POINTED AT A DEAD SOURCE.** `GET
/api/retail-admin/purchases/kitchen-source` and `POST .../copy-from-kitchen` pull a
`scope='kitchen'` PO into an editable retail draft, with a picker in
`16-purchasing.js`, a `copied_from_po_id` link, a 409 on a second copy, and an
all-or-nothing batch. §78 deleted the app that produced those kitchen POs, so **that
machine works and has nothing left to draw from.** This section gives it a live source
rather than inventing a second one beside it.

**WHAT WAS ACTUALLY MISSING WAS THE DOOR.** The cooks are `tenant_users` on `/m` holding
`quickstock:add`, `restock:fulfil` and `production:log`. They have no screen that says
"we are out of flour", and no table that could hold the sentence if they did.

### PART ONE — B: THE SEND DOES NOT CREATE A PURCHASE ORDER

**A REQUEST IS NOT A PURCHASE, AND THE GAP BETWEEN THEM IS WHERE THE BUYER WORKS.** A PO
posts to `expense_entries` the moment it reaches Ordered and writes the material's price
back on the same transition — verified on this date against
`postRetailPOExpenses`, whose postable set is `['Ordered','Delivered']`, and against the
`firePriceAlertsForPO` call on the status route. **Ash raised this himself and was
right.** So a send that created a PO would let a cook's tap reach the books, and would
have to guess a supplier, a price and a store that nobody has chosen yet.

**THE REQUEST THEREFORE LANDS AS DEMAND, and the buyer converts it.** The kitchen sends;
Purchasing shows the outstanding lines; the buyer ticks what they want, presses once, and
gets a **Draft** RPO with the lines already filled. Supplier, price and store are theirs,
and Order is theirs. **Nothing is retyped, and nothing is posted by anyone but the buyer.**

**"AUTOMATIC" IS THEREFORE ABOUT THE TYPING, NOT ABOUT THE AUTHORITY**, and that
distinction is the whole of Part One.

### PART TWO — THE LINE IS THE UNIT OF SOURCING, NOT THE REQUEST

The copy-from-kitchen bridge marks a whole PO copied. **This one marks a LINE sourced**,
and the request's status is the rollup — the same grain change §61 made to the kitchen
queue, for the same reason it made it there. A buyer splits a morning's flour and oil
across two suppliers as a matter of course; a request that could only be converted whole
would force one PO per supplier per request, or force the buyer to delete lines out of a
draft they did not want.

**A LINE IS SOURCED ONCE.** `sourced_po_id` on the item is the record and the refusal:
ticking a line that already carries one is refused, so two buyers working the same list
cannot raise the same flour twice.

### PART THREE — A NEW TABLE PAIR. NOT `restock_items`, AND NOT `kitchen_orders`

**NOT `restock_items`, THOUGH IT IS THE OBVIOUS REUSE.** That rail is product-shaped —
`product_id` FKs `products`, and every surface on it (pick, dispatch, `goods_state`,
`stock_applied_at`, Ready from the kitchen, the print path) assumes a subject with a stock
table behind it. **Materials have no stock table**, deliberately: §32's addendum deferred
material stock and §39 declined to grant it. Carrying a material on that rail means an
"unless this line is a material" branch in every one of those places, which is the shape
that produces a screen quietly doing nothing.

**NOT `kitchen_orders` / `kitchen_order_items` EITHER, and this is the trap worth naming.**
They are in the schema, they already carry `ingredient_id`, `qty`, `unit` and a
`ko_number`, they are the old app's ingredient requisition, and they have **no reader
left** — `audit_made_materials.js` counts them and nothing else. They look free. But
`kitchen_orders.created_by` FKs `users(id)`, the realm §81 retired, and that is precisely
the defect `restock_orders`'s own header records as having broken restock for every
non-Roots tenant with *"no such table: main.users"* once foreign keys were enforced.
**Reviving a table also inherits the meaning of whatever rows it holds.** New tables,
`created_by` a plain audit integer with no FK, exactly as `restock_orders` and
`production_batches` were repaired to be.

**THE OLD PAIR IS NOT DELETED HERE.** They retire on their own change, with the rest of
the legacy schema; deleting them inside a feature build would widen this ruling into that
cleanup. They are recorded as dead so the next reader does not mistake this section for
having missed them.

### PART FOUR — THE QUANTITY IS IN `ingredients.buy_unit`, AND THAT IS NOT A CHOICE MADE HERE

Ash: *"they order according to the unit setup of that material, it's already part of the
material setting."* **He is describing what the system already does.** The material record
carries **Buy unit · 采购单位** (`ingredients.buy_unit`) beside its recipe unit, and a
material line on a retail PO already defaults its unit to it — `16-purchasing.js`'s
material picker, whose own comment states the reason: **the price write-back only fires
when the line's unit matches `ingredients.buy_unit`.** A request that captured grams would
either be converted on the way into the PO or would silently break the write-back.

**SO THE REQUEST STORES `buy_unit` AND THE CONVERSION IS THE IDENTITY.** The cook counts
bags because a bag is what the material says it is bought in, and the line reaches the PO
unchanged. **No unit arithmetic exists anywhere on this path, and none should be added.**

### PART FIVE — THE GRANT, AND WHERE THE SCREEN LIVES

**A NEW CAPABILITY, HELD BY THE `kitchen` PRESET.** It is not folded into
`materials:view`: that key is the back-office masterlist — view, costs, edit — and a cook
who may ask for flour has no business being handed the buy prices of everything the
company purchases. The request's own picker serves the list, exactly as `production:log`
lets a cook choose a `store_product` without holding `products:view`.

**IT IS NOT `restock:request` EITHER**, though the two read alike. That key opens *Ask for
stock* and *Ask the kitchen*, which move existing goods between Roots' own locations and
spend nothing. This one asks the company to spend money with a supplier. Granting it
through the transfers key would mean every store operator who can request a delivery can
also raise procurement demand.

**SECTION `production`, GATED ON THE `production` FEATURE SWITCH** — Ash's *"it should be
part of production module"*, taken literally: the same switch that already gates Materials
and Recipes, so a tenant that makes nothing never sees the screen. Its capability sits in
the `production` section beside `production:log`, which is now the two things the kitchen
does.

### Rejected

**A LOW-STOCK TRIGGER, IN THE SHAPE OF `/api/retail-admin/reorder`.** That endpoint
compares `retail_store_stock.physical_qty` against a safety buffer, and **materials have
neither column** — there is nothing to compare. Auto-raising material demand needs
material stock, which §39 has declined twice. Somebody looks at the shelf and types it, and
that is the honest state rather than a gap.

**APPENDING TO AN EXISTING DRAFT PO INSTEAD OF MAKING A NEW ONE.** Considered because a
buyer working one supplier all morning would rather add to what is open. Refused for now
on the copy-from-kitchen precedent, which also always makes a new draft: appending needs a
rule for what happens when the target's supplier, store or status has moved on since it
was chosen, and that rule is worth its own decision rather than being assumed inside this
one.

**LETTING THE KITCHEN SEE PRICES ON THE REQUEST SCREEN.** A material's buy price is
`materials:costs`, a `money: 'shows'` grant. The request needs a name, a SKU, a unit and a
number; it does not need what the last bag cost, and putting it there would hand the whole
cost book to a role that was deliberately not given it.

### What this does NOT decide

**Whether the buyer can edit a requested quantity before converting.** The draft is
editable after conversion by the ordinary PUT, which covers the need; a "change it in the
request" path would need to say what the kitchen is told afterwards, and nothing yet asks
for it.

**What the kitchen is told when a line is sourced.** The status is visible on the request,
and no push, no dot and no Ready-style acknowledgement is built. §66 and §69 are the
precedent for adding one later if the morning turns out to need it; inventing it in advance
would be inventing the workflow rather than serving it.

## §87 — WHAT AN EMPLOYEE SPENDS IS A CLAIM UNTIL SOMEONE APPROVES IT; ONLY THEN IS IT AN EXPENSE

Ruling (Ash, 2026-09-09), on four questions put to him after a read-only survey of what
Finance already holds. **B**, of the two readings put to him for where a submitted expense
lives — **a claim table of its own, with nothing in the books until approval**, rather than
a status column on `expense_entries`. And **yes** three times: **a shop column on the
expense**, **an operating / non-operating flag on the tenant's expense categories**, and
**an approver may approve their own claim**.

The case that opened it, in Ash's own examples: an owner taking a private transfer, a
driver paying for a taxi on a work run, and the general class of small irregular spending
by staff that today reaches the monthly accounts only if somebody remembers to type it in.

### What already exists, and is not built here

**THE LEDGER, THE ROLLUP AND THE NORMALISER ARE DONE.** `expense_entries` (`schema.sql:272`
on this date — date, amount, category, description, `po_id`, `created_at`, `created_by`,
plus `payment_method` and `updated_at` added by migration at `database.js:1152` and
`:1160`). `routes/finance-transactions.js` is the typed write surface and the CSV the
bookkeeper works from; `routes/finance-summary.js` sums the ledger over any window with a
category breakdown ordered by weight; `storeCategory()` (`lib/category-text.js:153`) snaps
a typed category onto an existing one so three people typing rent do not produce three
lines. **An approved claim needs no new accounting surface — it needs to land here.**

**THE PROJECTION PATTERN IS DONE TOO, and this section copies it rather than inventing one
beside it.** A purchase order is a document with a life of its own that posts rows into
`expense_entries` carrying `po_id`, and those rows refuse edit and delete in the ledger
(`ERR.poEdit` / `ERR.poDelete` in `routes/finance-transactions.js`). A claim is the same
shape of thing: a document that becomes money when someone with authority says so.

**THE PHONE IS DONE.** Staff are `tenant_users` on `public/m.html`, and `screenWaste()` is
the exact precedent — an employee records something small, irregular and attributable, in
seconds, on a phone they already have installed.

**RECEIPT READING IS DONE.** `lib/alipay-ocr.js` reads a payment screenshot with a vision
model and is fail-soft by construction. Photographing a taxi receipt needs no new
infrastructure.

**WHAT WAS ACTUALLY MISSING IS FOUR THINGS.**

1. **No door.** Every finance write is `requireRetailAdmin`, and there is no finance screen
   on `/m` at all. A driver who paid ¥38 has no way to tell the system, on any device.
2. **No tenant-managed category list — the thing Ash asked for by name.** `categories`
   has a `kind='accounting'`, but the admin CRUD in `routes/retail.js` serves
   `kind='product'` only, nothing seeds it and nothing writes to it. The expense form's
   suggestions are instead derived from the categories already on rows on screen
   (`public/retail-admin/22-finance.js`). **So the category list is the accumulated history
   of what people typed, and the first typo is a permanent option.**
3. **No way to say the business owes an employee money.** `created_by` records who typed
   the row, not who was out of pocket. A taxi on the company account and a taxi from
   somebody's own wallet are the same row today.
4. **No location** — §36's own open column, below.

### PART ONE — B: THE CLAIM IS ITS OWN TABLE, AND NOTHING REACHES THE BOOKS UNTIL APPROVAL

**The case that separates the two readings.** Monday 09:00 a driver submits a ¥38 taxi.
Nobody has approved it. Tuesday 08:00 the owner opens the month.

*Reading A — a status column on `expense_entries`.* The ¥38 is in the ledger from the
moment of submission, and **every reader has to remember to exclude it**: the Summary's
operating-expense sum, its category breakdown, the Transactions list, the CSV export. Miss
one and money nobody approved is in the accounts — **and the miss is silent**, which is the
same defect §36 names when it says a filter that returns a wrong answer is worse than no
filter. Rejected claims then stay in the ledger for good as rows every future query must
step around.

*Reading B — a claim table.* The ¥38 is not in the ledger, so it cannot appear anywhere. On
approval **one row is written into `expense_entries` carrying `claim_id`**, on the `po_id`
pattern. A rejected claim never touches the books at all.

**B IS THE RULING, and the reason is that the invariant holds by construction rather than
by everyone remembering.** No existing finance screen learns a new condition.

**THE POSTED ROW IS A PROJECTION AND IS REFUSED FOR EDIT IN THE LEDGER, exactly as a PO row
is** — the claim is the record, and a value typed onto its projection would be lost on the
next re-post.

**ONE INTEGRATION TRAP, NAMED NOW SO IT IS NOT DISCOVERED LATER.** The hand-typed read in
`readTransactions` selects money out with `WHERE po_id IS NULL`. A claim-posted row satisfies
that predicate, so it would arrive on the Transactions screen looking hand-typed and freely
editable, and an edit there would be silently undone by the next re-post. **The predicate
becomes "no `po_id` AND no `claim_id`", and that is an edit to a shipped file, not new code
beside it.**

**WHAT B COSTS, STATED PLAINLY:** one extra table, one posting step, and a
delete-and-re-post when an approved claim is edited. Roughly a day, once.

### PART TWO — THE TENANT'S EXPENSE CATEGORIES BECOME A MANAGED LIST, AND EACH CARRIES ONE FLAG

`kind='accounting'` gets create / rename / reorder / deactivate in Settings, on the shape
`routes/retail.js` already serves for product categories. **THE LIST SHIPS EMPTY.** §36's
rule stands unchanged — no defaults and no seed, because an empty list cannot offer a wrong
option, and the four the kitchen app defaulted to are what produced the ¥152,309 mis-filing
that rule was written for.

**EACH CATEGORY CARRIES ONE FLAG: does this count as an operating expense.** The case is
the owner's private transfer. ¥5,000 leaving the account is real money and belongs in the
record; it is **not** a cost of running the shop. Summed with rent and wages it takes ¥5,000
off the month's Net, **and nothing on the screen looks wrong** — the same failure the
category normaliser exists to prevent, one level up.

**A CATEGORY THAT ROWS REFERENCE IS DEACTIVATED, NEVER DELETED.** An expense row stores its
category as TEXT and the flag lives on the category record, so the two are joined by name.
Delete the private-expenses category and every row that named it silently becomes an
operating expense again — **five thousand yuan re-entering the month's costs with no event
to see.** Deactivation hides it from the form and keeps the flag readable, which is the
rule §18 already applies to archiving elsewhere.

**THE SUMMARY MUST THEREFORE SPLIT, and that is a change to a shipped screen rather than a
new one.** `routes/finance-summary.js` sums every row in the window today. Once a category
can be non-operating, the operating line excludes it **and the excluded amount is shown on
its own line rather than dropped** — a number that disappears from a total without saying
so is the same defect wearing different clothes.

### PART THREE — THE LOCATION COLUMN LANDS ON `expense_entries`, AND §36'S OPEN QUESTION IS CLOSED

§36's *An expense may carry a location, and blank means the whole business* (DECIDED
2026-09-01) settled the dimension and left "where the column goes, and its shape"
explicitly undecided. **It is decided here: `store_id INTEGER`, nullable, on
`expense_entries`, referencing `retail_stores(id)`** — the shape the rest of the schema
already uses — **and the same column on the claim**, defaulted from the submitter's store
scope, which the RBAC layer already computes as `scopeStores`.

**NULL KEEPS §36's MEANING EXACTLY**: the cost belongs to the business, not to any one
place. **Nothing is backfilled.** Every existing row is NULL, which reads as business-wide,
which is what those rows always meant — there is no migration to get wrong.

**THIS UNBLOCKS THE SUMMARY'S STORE FILTER AND ITS CONTRIBUTION ROW**, refused since
2026-09-02 for the one reason that revenue could be store-scoped and expenses could not.
**Building that filter is NOT this section's work** and remains §36's, including its rule
that the filtered view says Contribution and never Net. What this section owes it is the
column.

### PART FOUR — WHO PAID, AND WHAT IS OWED, ARE TWO DIFFERENT FACTS

**Who paid** reuses `payment_method` — already a column on `expense_entries`, already a
tenant-editable list (`categories` `kind='payment_method'`, seeded at `database.js:898`
with the three account types) — with one addition that list does not have today: **the
employee's own money.**

**What is owed** is a settlement state **on the claim, not on the ledger row**. A claim paid
from the company account owes nobody and is finished at approval. A claim paid from a
pocket is a debt to a named person until it is settled.

**THE REIMBURSEMENT IS NOT A SECOND EXPENSE.** The ¥38 is one cost, recorded once, at
approval. Paying the driver back moves money between the business and a person and **posts
nothing to the ledger** — a system that wrote a row for it would report ¥76 of taxis.

### PART FIVE — WHO MAY SUBMIT, WHO MAY APPROVE, AND SELF-APPROVAL IS ALLOWED

**Two new capabilities — submit and approve — and NOT `finance:record`.** That grant is
money-marked and opens the whole ledger; the staff floor presets carry no finance
capability at all and deliberately withhold even `waste:costs` from the people who record
waste (`lib/capabilities.js`). **A ¥38 taxi must not be the reason a driver can read the
books.**

**AN APPROVER MAY APPROVE THEIR OWN CLAIM — Ash — and it is the right answer for the
business rather than a relaxation.** In a shop with one manager, the person who spends and
the person who approves are the same person. A rule forbidding it does not produce a second
approver; it produces an unusable screen and spending recorded somewhere outside the
system. **The guard is the record, not the refusal**: the approver is stored on the claim,
shown on the row, and both events already reach the activity log. **A self-approval is
visible; blocked spending is invisible.**

### What is NOT decided here, named so it is not read as done

- **How the receipt image is stored.** The precedent is `supplier_documents.data` — a
  base64 data URI in the tenant database — and receipts arrive at a volume suppliers'
  licences never did. The claim carries a receipt; where the bytes live is a build decision
  with its own argument.
- **OCR prefill.** `lib/alipay-ocr.js` can read amount and date off a photograph, and it is
  fail-soft by design. It is a later slice, and **a human confirms every figure** — an OCR
  that quietly sets an amount is a wrong number nobody typed.
- **Recurring or scheduled expenses**, spending limits per role, and any approval chain
  beyond one approver. None of them are needed by the cases that opened this section.
- **Strings.** No Chinese is minted here. The build composes under `docs/tacet-delivery-vocabulary.md`
  Rule 4 as amended 2026-09-06, preferring the pairs Finance already ships.

### Build order — one PR per step

1. **Expense categories in Settings**, with the operating flag, and the Summary split that
   flag requires. This is the foundation; nothing below is worth much without it.
2. **The claim table and the phone submit screen** — category, amount, who paid, optional
   photo, submit.
3. **The approval list and the posting step**, including the `claim_id` predicate fix in
   `readTransactions` and the `store_id` column.
4. **Settlement** — what is owed to whom, and marking it paid.
5. **OCR prefill**, last, because it is the only part that is a convenience rather than a
   capability.

### BUILT 2026-09-09 — step one, and the two questions it had to settle

Categories in Settings, the operating flag, and the Summary split. `database.js`
adds `is_operating` and `is_active` to `categories` (both `DEFAULT 1`, so every
category that exists today is an operating expense and the Summary is unchanged
until a tenant says otherwise); `routes/finance-categories.js` is the CRUD;
`routes/finance-summary.js` splits; the screen is a third sub-view on Finance.
`scripts/test_finance_categories.js` is the suite.

**THE FLAG IS RESOLVED ON `spacingKey`, NOT ON A SQL JOIN, and that is worth the
sentence.** The expense row holds its category as free text and the flag lives on
the `categories` record, so the two are matched by name — and `lib/category-text.js`
is this product's one rule for when two category strings are the same category.
A `=` join would read `Private expense` and `private expense ` as two different
things and put one of them back into operating expenses, **silently, which is the
exact failure the flag exists to prevent.** The suite pins it with a row whose
spelling drifted from the list's.

Two questions the section did not answer, settled here because the build could
not proceed without them:

**THE FORM FALLS BACK TO THE OLD DERIVATION WHILE THE LIST IS EMPTY.** §36's
empty-list rule is about not offering a WRONG option, and a category read off
this tenant's own ledger rows is not one. Ripping the suggestions out on the day
this ships would leave a business with three years of expenses typing every
category from memory, to no benefit — the tenant has a list the moment they add
one entry, and from then on it is the only thing offered. So: the tenant's own
list when it has anything in it, the derived set when it does not.

**HIDING REACHES THE MATERIALS FORM TOO.** `GET
/api/retail-admin/materials/meta/accounting-categories` offers the same
`kind='accounting'` list on the material record, and it now filters to active
entries. Hiding a category means it stops being OFFERED; a second surface going
on offering it would file new rows under a name the tenant has retired. Nothing
existing is touched — a material already carrying a retired category keeps it.

### BUILT 2026-09-09 — step two, and the screen Ash chose

The claim table and the phone's submit screen. `schema.sql` gains
`staff_expenses`; `lib/expense-claim.js` is the validator; `routes/staff-expenses.js`
is the submit, the person's own list and the receipt fetch; `public/m.html` gains
an **Expense** row in Operations and the screen behind it.
`scripts/test_staff_expenses.js` is the suite.

**THE SCREEN IS OPTION A — ONE CARD, EVERY FIELD VISIBLE.** Three were drawn
against Tacet's own tokens in `reference/expense-capture-mockup.html` and put to
Ash: one card, an amount-first number pad, and a grid of category tiles. He chose
the first. **The other two are not kept as options.** A trial switch offering all
three was proposed and dropped the moment he answered: three ways to record one
thing is a product with no answer to "how do I record an expense", and the
mockup file is the record of the alternatives, which is what a mockup is for.

**FIELD ORDER IS THE ORDER SOMEBODY BESIDE A TAXI ACTUALLY ASKS**: how much, what
for, whose money. The photo, the note, the date and the shop follow, because each
is optional and none is what the person opened the screen to type.

**THE ONE SENTENCE THE SCREEN CANNOT DO WITHOUT** sits under the button: *this is
not recorded in the accounts until it is approved*. Part one is a decision about
which table a claim lives in; that line is the same decision told to the person
it affects, in the words the phone already uses for money reaching the books.

Four things the build had to settle:

**THE VALIDATOR IS A PURE MODULE, AND THAT WAS LEARNED THE EXPENSIVE WAY.** It
began inside the route, and the suite that wanted to RUN its rules — a closed
set, a rounding, two size limits, all of them things a grep can be made to pass
while the code is wrong — had to `require` the route, which boots express and the
database behind it. It did, and left the dev database in a state that turned
`test_restock_urgent.js` red. `lib/expense-claim.js` is the answer, on the shape
`lib/category-text.js` already had.

**THE PHOTO IS DOWNSCALED ON THE PHONE AND BOUNDED ON THE SERVER.** A camera
hands over 4–8 MB, base64 adds a third again, and a year of those is a tenant
database nobody can copy. 1280px on the long edge at quality 0.7 is a receipt a
person can read; the server refuses anything over 2 MB rather than truncating,
because half a photograph stored is a receipt nobody can read on a claim that
looks like it has one.

**A CLAIM IS PERSONAL, AND THE OWNERSHIP TEST IS IN THE QUERY.** The list reads
`WHERE submitted_by IS ?` and the receipt route matches owner and id together —
a fetch-then-compare is one early return away from serving anybody's photograph
of anybody's spending.

**WHAT THE SHOP OWES IS NOT THE SUM OF WHAT WAS SENT**: approved, own money, not
yet settled. A submitted claim might be rejected and a company-account one owes
nobody, so the figure is computed in the route rather than on the phone — the day
a second surface wants it, the rule is in one place.

**THE CAPABILITY IS `expenses:submit`, AND THE APPROVING KEY IS NOT REGISTERED.**
A key in the matrix that gates nothing is a permission an owner ticks and sees no
effect from. `lib/roles.js migrateExpenseSubmitCap` backfills the new key onto
EVERY existing role, with no untouched-role guard, on the argument its sibling
proved on production three commits earlier: that guard protects a decision an
admin made by unticking something, and nobody can have unticked a key that did
not exist yesterday. Every role, because saying what you spent is not a power
over anything — the narrowing that matters is on approval.

**One test guard was widened deliberately rather than stepped over.**
`test_kitchen_queue_reachable.js` asserts the kitchen role gains nothing outside
its own work; `expenses:submit` is admitted by name, on the grounds that the same
role already holds `production:request` — which asks the company to place a
purchase order with a supplier — and saying "I spent ¥38 of my own money" is
strictly less than that. The argument is written into the assertion, and
`expenses:approve` must still turn it red.

### BUILT 2026-09-09 — step three, and the money reaches the books

The approval list, the posting step, the `claim_id` predicate fix and the
`store_id` column. `lib/expense-posting.js` is the posting; the decide route and
the queue are in `routes/staff-expenses.js`; the screen is **Approvals** on `/m`,
gated on `expenses:approve`.

**THE APPROVAL SCREEN IS ON THE PHONE, NOT IN THE BACK OFFICE**, and that is a
choice rather than an omission. The person who approves a ¥38 taxi is a manager
or an owner standing in a shop, and §81 is the long record of what happens when
the people who do a job have no login for the screen that does it. The back
office is not left out of it: the posted rows appear on the Transactions ledger
the moment they are approved, which is where the money is read.

**POSTING IS `postRetailPOExpenses`'s SHAPE, DELIBERATELY.** Delete every
`expense_entries` row carrying this claim's id, then insert from the document as
it now stands. So approving twice re-posts rather than double-posting, and
rejecting after approving REMOVES the row — §36 decided a hand-typed row is
freely deletable because "mistakes here are typos", and an approval given by
accident is the same kind of mistake. An offsetting entry would turn a two-row
ledger into four rows nobody can read.

**THE CLAIM'S STATUS AND ITS LEDGER ROW MOVE IN ONE TRANSACTION**, and the post
reads the row AFTER the update rather than the one loaded before it: a claim that
says approved with nothing behind it, or a row with no claim, is a discrepancy
nobody would find until the month did not add up.

**`created_by` ON THE POSTED ROW IS THE APPROVER, NOT THE SPENDER.** That column
has always meant *who put this in the books*, and the approver is who did. Who
spent the money is in the description — the name, then the note — because a ¥38
line with no supplier, no invoice and no purchase order behind it is answerable
three months later only if it says whose taxi it was.

**THE TRAP §87 NAMED IN ADVANCE IS CLOSED.** `readTransactions` selected
hand-typed money out with `po_id IS NULL`, which a claim-posted row satisfies —
it would have arrived on the Transactions screen looking freely editable, and the
edit would have been undone by the next decision. The predicate is now
`po_id IS NULL AND claim_id IS NULL`, `loadTyped` refuses a claim row with its own
wording, and the screen tints it and drops the Edit link. The client's
`row.source !== 'po'` became `=== 'manual'` for the same reason: with one kind of
projection those read alike, and with two the negation is the bug.

**`store_id` LANDS ON `expense_entries` AND NOTHING IS BACKFILLED.** §36's open
column is closed; every existing row is NULL, which is what those rows always
meant. **The Summary's store filter is NOT built here** — it is §36's, including
its rule that a filtered view says Contribution and never Net. What this step
owed it was the column.

**ONE EXCEPTION TO THE FAIL-OPEN CONTRACT, and it is the only one.**
`lib/cap-routes.js` gates mutations only where a tenant has switched
`rbac_enforce` on, which is off by default and right for a screen somebody is
mid-shift on. On this route it would mean that on every tenant, anybody who can
raise a claim can approve their own. `requireApprover` therefore refuses in the
route as well — including when the capability set cannot be resolved, because a
money route does not fall open on an unanswered question. The cap-routes rule for
`/decide` also sits ABOVE the general one; below it, every submitter would be an
approver.

**SELF-APPROVAL IS ALLOWED AND MARKED.** Part five's decision, made visible: the
row says `本人提交` rather than the button refusing. The approver is stored, shown
and logged, and the activity row records whether the decision was on the
approver's own claim.

Still to come: **settlement** — marking what the shop owes an employee as paid
back. It POSTS NOTHING when it lands, and the suite already asserts the shape it
must not take.

### BUILT 2026-09-09 — step four, and §87 is complete

Settlement. `POST /staff-expenses/:id/settle` writes one column; the **Owed to
your team** block sits above the approvals queue and marks a person's claims paid
together.

**IT POSTS NOTHING, WHICH IS THE WHOLE OF IT.** The ¥38 was recorded once, at
approval. Paying the driver back moves money between the business and a person,
and a system that wrote a second row for it would report ¥76 of taxis. The suite
asserts the handler touches `expense_entries` in no way at all.

**WHAT IT IS FOR is a question the ledger cannot answer**: the books know the shop
spent ¥38 on transport; they do not know the ¥38 is still in a driver's pocket.

**THE ROW IS A PERSON, NOT A CLAIM**, because that is how it is paid — one
transfer to Wei, not four. The total carries the ids behind it and the phone
settles them in sequence rather than in parallel: four writes racing on a shop's
wifi is how two of them land.

**THE OWED FIGURE IS COUNTED OVER EVERY CLAIM, NOT THE QUEUE'S PAGE.** The queue
is capped at 200 rows for the screen's sake; a debt does not stop existing
because it fell off the end of a list, so it has its own uncapped query. The
names read for the payload cover everybody either half of it mentions, or an
owed person whose last claim fell outside the queue would show a total with no
name against it.

**GATED ON `expenses:approve` RATHER THAN A KEY OF ITS OWN.** A third capability
would gate a single toggle, be granted to the same people, and add one more row
to a matrix somebody has to understand. Saying "we have paid Wei back" is an
assertion about money by the person who already decides money on this screen. If
it ever needs to belong to a bookkeeper who is not an approver, that is when the
key earns its place.

**ONLY A DEBT CAN BE SETTLED, and the two refusals are separate**: a claim that
is not approved yet might still be rejected, and one paid on the company account
owes nobody. A shared "cannot mark this paid" would send an operator looking for
a permission problem that is not there.

**UN-SETTLING EXISTS BECAUSE THE UN-APPROVE REFUSAL DEPENDS ON IT.** Step three
refuses to un-approve a settled claim — money has changed hands outside this
system — so a claim marked paid by mistake would be stuck for good if it could
not be un-marked. Both directions are logged.

§87 is built end to end: a category list, a claim, an approval that posts, and a
debt that clears. **What is deliberately still not built** is named in the section
above — OCR prefill on the receipt, recurring expenses, per-role spending limits,
and any approval chain beyond one approver. None of them is needed by the cases
that opened this section.

### AMENDED 2026-09-10 — the category control is a picker, not a wall of chips

Ash opened the live Expense screen and sent the screenshot: **thirty-one
categories rendered as chips, alphabetical, with the amount field pushed off the
top.** He was given three options in
`reference/expense-category-picker-mockup.html` and chose **B — a collapsed field
that opens a searchable picker, with what this person picked recently on top.**

**THE LAYOUT WAS THE SYMPTOM. THE CAUSE IS THAT THE PHONE WAS HANDED THE
BOOKKEEPER'S LIST.** Step two shipped the claim form offering every active
`kind='accounting'` category, on the reasoning that the tenant's own list is the
right list — which is true of Finance and false of a phone. Rent, wages, employee
social insurance, electricity, ingredients and protein powder are all real costs
that belong in the books, and **nobody raises one out of their own pocket.**

**WHY B AND NOT A.** Option A — a per-category *offer on the phone* tick — was
this session's own recommendation, because it fixes the cause rather than the
symptom. Ash chose the picker, and the choice is defensible on a ground the
recommendation undervalued: **A needs the shop to curate a second list and to
keep curating it**, and a category added later is invisible on the phone until
somebody remembers to tick it — a silent failure, on the screen where a silent
failure means an expense filed under the wrong name or not at all. B needs
nothing maintained and is correct at thirty-one categories or three hundred.
**A remains available and is not withdrawn**: it narrows what the picker offers
and can be added later without undoing anything built here.

**WHAT B DOES NOT FIX, recorded so it is not read as fixed**: every category is
still reachable, so a driver can still file a taxi under Salaries if they set out
to. The mockup says so in terms. That is a curation problem, and A is its answer.

**RECENTS ARE THIS PERSON'S OWN, AND THEY ARE THE POINT.** The picker's top
section is the categories this operator has claimed under before, newest first —
so the second claim anybody makes is two taps, and the alphabet stops deciding
what they see. **It is derived from their own claims and never from the shop's**:
a driver and an office manager do not want the same six, and a shop-wide "most
used" would hand the driver whatever the office manager files most.

**THE SEARCH BOX FOLLOWS THE HOUSE RULE THAT #437 AND ITS FOLLOW-UP ESTABLISHED**
— `oninput` stores the query and repaints ONLY the results box, never the app.
`render()` replaces the whole app in one `innerHTML`, and a rebuilt `<input>`
opens a fresh soft keyboard on its letter page: Ash reported that from the
kitchen, typing a SKU and getting one digit then the alphabet. A new search box
that called `render()` would be the fifth instance of a defect four screens were
just repaired for.

**TWO DUPLICATE PAIRS ARE RECORDED HERE AND NOT ACTED ON.** Putting the list on
one screen made it readable in one go for the first time, and it holds
`Marketing&Promotion 市场推广费用` beside `营销 Marketing`, and
`Kitchen low cost & non-durable equipment 厨房低值易耗品` beside
`low cost & non-durable equipment 低值易耗品`. Every expense filed under one of
each pair splits the monthly breakdown into two lines that read alike — §36's
three-rent-payments defect, arriving through the vocabulary rather than through a
typo. **Hiding one of each is the tenant's call and takes fifteen seconds on the
Categories screen**; this session did not make it, because which spelling
survives is a decision about the shop's books.

### FIXED 2026-09-10 — one language on screen, and a receipt that already exists

Two reports from Ash, both from the live screen.

**THE ENGLISH SCREEN WAS SHOWING BOTH LANGUAGES**, because a category is DATA and
not a locked pair. `T()` reaches every other string on that screen; the category
is a value the tenant typed, held as ONE free-text column with both halves glued
into it (§36), so `Logistics&Delivery 物流与配送费用` rendered whole. **The
desktop solved this on 2026-09-02 and the phone never got it** — the claim screen
was written months later and reached for the value directly.

`public/retail-admin/22-finance.js`'s `finCatSplit` / `finCatLabel` /
`finCatLabels` are **ported, not re-derived**: same regexes, same refusal to guess
on interleaved text, same collision rule. The two copies exist because one file is
a retail-admin bundle and the other a standalone document, and
`scripts/test_staff_expenses.js` now **runs both over the same values and asserts
they agree**, so the copy cannot drift.

**FIVE RENDER SITES, NOT ONE.** CLAUDE.md's rule — a finding is where it was
found, not the extent of the problem — applied literally: the collapsed row, the
picker, the receipt after a send, the submitter's own list and the approver's
queue all drew the raw value. All five go through the splitter now, and the suite
asserts none of them is left reaching for `r.category` directly.

**THE SEARCH STILL READS THE STORED VALUE, NEVER THE RENDERED HALF.** An English
operator typing `物流` and a Chinese one typing `logistics` both find the row.
Searching the half on screen would make half the vocabulary unreachable in each
language, which is a worse bug than the one being fixed.

**THE COLLISION RULE MATTERS HERE AND IS NOT HYPOTHETICAL.** The live list holds
`Marketing&Promotion 市场推广费用` beside `营销 Marketing`, whose English halves
read alike; both render WHOLE rather than drawing two rows nobody can tell apart.

**A STORE NAME FOLLOWS THE LIVE LANGUAGE TOO.** The Shop chips shipped as
`name_cn || name_en`, which put Chinese on an English screen for any store named
in both. The fallback ACROSS is kept: a store named in one language only shows
that name rather than a number.

**AND THE PHOTO CAN COME FROM THE GALLERY.** The file input carried
`capture="environment"`, which makes Android open the camera and offer nothing
else — so a receipt already photographed, screenshotted, or sent by a supplier
could not be attached at all, which is most of them. The attribute is gone;
`accept="image/*"` is what keeps the chooser to pictures.

## §88 — A LINE OF THE BREAKDOWN OPENS ONTO THE ROWS BEHIND IT

**Decided 2026-09-10 by Ash**, from the live Summary card: *"there should be an
option to click on each category and see details payment break down."*

### The question the operator arrives with

The disclosure on the operating-expenses row says Ingredients cost ¥27,081 and
then stops. The next question — *which purchases were those* — has no answer on
the card, and the operator's only route to one is to leave for the Transactions
tab and read a ledger that is not organised by the thing they clicked.

### THE OBVIOUS BUILD IS WRONG, AND THAT IS THE DECISION

Filtering the Transactions list to the clicked category is one line of client
code and it **shows a smaller number than the line it opened from.**

`routes/finance-transactions.js` collapses PO-derived rows to **one row per
purchase order**. A purchase order buys several categories at once, so the
collapsed row carries no category at all — `category: null` — and no category
filter can match it. It also windows those rows on the **purchase order's own
date**, where the breakdown windows on the expense row's. Ingredients is exactly
the category most likely to be mostly purchase orders, so the drill-down would
have opened ¥27,081 onto a list totalling whatever happened to be hand-typed,
with the purchases missing and nothing on screen to say so.

§36 already names this as the worst thing this card can do — a figure whose own
breakdown does not add up. **Borrowing a list that was reshaped for a different
question is how that happens**, and the reshaping is correct where it lives: a
purchase is one fact on a ledger a bookkeeper is reading.

### WHAT IS BUILT INSTEAD

`GET /api/retail-admin/finance/summary/category?from=&to=&category=` — **the
breakdown's own query with the `GROUP BY` removed.** Same table, same window
expression, same category match; listed instead of summed. The detail therefore
totals the figure that was clicked **by construction rather than by agreement**,
and there is no second place for the two to drift apart.

PO rows are listed **individually**. PO-0050 appearing twice inside one category
is not a duplicate: it bought that category on two lines, and both are inside the
total. The PO number rides along so the row still says where it came from.

### THE MATCH IS ON RAW TEXT, NOT ON `spacingKey`

The breakdown groups by the category column **as stored**, so
`Ingredients(Kitchen+Retail Use)` and `Ingredients (Kitchen + Retail Use)` are
two lines on the card, each with its own figure. §87's `is_operating` resolution
matches those on `spacingKey`; the breakdown pointedly does not merge them for
display.

**A detail read keyed on `spacingKey` would gather both spellings under either
line and overshoot the figure clicked.** The rule that keeps this honest is
*match what the `GROUP BY` grouped*: `=` against the raw text, which shares
BINARY collation with it — the column carries no `COLLATE`.

### `NULLIF(category, '')` — a pre-existing defect fixed here

SQLite groups `''` and `NULL` apart, while the payload maps both to `null` and
the screen draws both as "Not recorded". A tenant holding one of each therefore
rendered **two identical lines with different figures**, and the drill-down had
two buckets to disagree with.

The fold is `NULLIF`, never `TRIM`. `TRIM` would merge ` Ingredients` onto
`Ingredients` and decide a question about typography that `lib/category-text.js`
deliberately refuses to. Nothing about the totals moves: the same rows are summed
either way.

### NO ROW CEILING

A capped list is a list that does not add up, which is the one guarantee this
endpoint makes. `readTransactions` caps at 2,000 because it is a browsable
ledger; this is one category inside one window. **If the volume ever justifies a
ceiling, the answer is paging with the total stated — never a silent slice.**

### READ-ONLY, AND THE REASON IS RECORDED

The rows disclose and do not edit. Editing lives on the Transactions tab, where
the refusals for PO- and claim-derived rows already are (§36, §87 step three).
Opening a second write path into `expense_entries` while a concurrent session was
settling who may edit and cancel a transaction is how two rules about one table
come to disagree.

**No link out from a detail row**, unlike Transactions' PO link. The row is
inside a figure, not a ledger the operator is working, and the tab that carries
the link is one click away.

### NO NEW CHINESE

Nothing is composed. Every pair the rows render — `采购单自动记入`,
`费用申请 · 个人支付`, `费用申请`, `加载中…`, `暂无记录`,
`财务数据加载失败。` — already ships on the Transactions or Approvals sub-view of
the same file, for the same fact about the same kind of row. **A test asserts it**
rather than a commit message claiming it: each string must appear at least twice
in `22-finance.js`, so a "reuse" that is really a mint fails the build.

The delegation of `docs/tacet-delivery-vocabulary.md` Rule 4 (amended
2026-09-06) is therefore not exercised, and nothing is owed to that document.


### AMENDED 2026-09-10 — and a purchase-order row opens onto its items

**Asked for by Ash** from the working drill-down: *"what about collapsing if i
want of each po to see the exact item?"* A third level, and the last one there
is: category → purchase-order row → the items on it.

**It is this section's own trap one level down, and it takes the same answer.**
A purchase order buys several categories at once and the poster writes ONE
EXPENSE ROW PER CATEGORY, so `RPO-0017 · 3 lines · ¥1,230` is **three of that
order's lines**, not the order. RPO-0017 may hold twelve. Listing all twelve
would show a list that does not add up to the row it opened from — the same
defect, arriving a third time by a third road.

So `GET /api/retail-admin/finance/summary/po-lines` is the poster's own grouped
query with the `GROUP BY` removed and one group selected, exactly as
`/summary/category` is to the breakdown. **Three levels, one rule, applied three
times.**

#### The row is addressed by its ledger id

One `expense_entries` row IS one (purchase order, category) pair, so its id names
the group with nothing for a client to get wrong. Passing the pair would let a
caller ask for a combination no row was posted for and receive a plausible list
totalling a figure that appears on no screen. **The category is read off the row,
never accepted from the request.**

#### Billable quantity, never `qty`

`billableQtySql` from `lib/po-returns.js` — what turned up less what went back,
the expression both posters bill on — **referenced, never restated.** A reader
using `qty` prices a returned item at what it cost before it went back, which is
not what the figure above it counted. A partly returned line shows the smaller
quantity; a fully returned one is not in the list at all, because it is not in
the money either.

#### The blank-category fallback differs by realm

A line with no category posts as `门店进货 Retail stock` from
`postRetailPOExpenses` and as `未分类 Uncategorized` from `postPOExpenses`. Both
realms write into this one ledger and are told apart only by
`purchase_orders.scope`, so the fallback is **resolved per row, in SQL, from the
order's own scope.** Binding either label across a mixed read files the other
realm's blank lines under a name they were never posted with.

**The two literals are copied into the reader, which this file normally
forbids.** Lifting them into a shared module means editing two posters that WRITE
MONEY inside a change that only reads. So they are copied and pinned by a test
that reads both shipped posters and fails if either string moves. That buys the
drift protection without touching the write path. **If a third poster ever
appears, lift them properly.**

#### The landed-cost row gets no chevron

Freight, tax and handling post as their own expense row against the order with no
`po_line_items` behind them. The server counts the lines and the client draws a
control only where there is one — **this screen's existing rule, that a chevron
opening onto nothing is a control that lies, applied rather than restated.** The
row still renders and still counts; §36 hides no money.

#### A price is not a period total

The first draft rendered the unit cost with `finMoney`, which renders whole
units. **A ¥3.50 jar drew as ¥4** — correct for a period total and a lie about
what the supplier charged.

`public/retail-admin/01-core.js` already states the rule: *"anywhere an operator
might reconcile the number against something — a list, a total, a dialog, an
export — uses acMoney and shows the real amount."* So the inline arithmetic
(`200 pc × ¥3.50`) is `acMoney`, while **the aligned figure column stays
`finMoney` at all three levels** — that column is the staircase's own, its
magnitude is §36's decision, and a list that switched to fen halfway down would
stop lining up under the total it exists to be checked against.

For the same reason the payload does not pass a unit cost through `fen()`: **a
price can be sub-cent** (`lib/money` keeps `toMicro`/`fromMicro` and `acMoney`
takes a `dp` override for exactly these), and rounding it server-side destroys
the value to save nothing.

#### Rounding, stated rather than discovered

The poster rounds **once over the group** (audit I-02), so `lines_total` is
computed the same way and equals the posted figure exactly — asserted by a test.

**Allocating the rounded total across the lines with `splitMinor` was
REJECTED.** It would print a line at a price the supplier never charged, and a
purchase-order line's truth is quantity times unit cost.

> **CORRECTED 2026-09-10, same day — the paragraph that stood here was wrong,
> and is quoted rather than deleted per this file's convention.** It read:
> *"Per-line display rounding can differ by a cent on a three-decimal unit
> price. The card renders whole yuan so it does not surface."*
>
> **Both sentences are false, and the second is backwards.** Rendering whole
> yuan is not what hides the drift, it is what CREATES it. `finMoney` rounds
> each line by up to half a yuan and the errors accumulate — the error is
> per-line and unbounded in the number of lines, not "a cent" on an unusual
> price. See the amendment below.

#### AMENDED — whole yuan on the staircase, fen below it

**Reported by Ash off the live card**, and settled by arithmetic rather than
taste. His four packaging lines:

```
true line amounts : 52.80  47.60  145.60  13.40   →  259.40
shown whole       : 53     48     146     13      →  260
row shown whole   :                                   259
```

Same rows, two whole numbers a yuan apart, and nothing on screen to explain it.
A random sweep over realistic orders found **¥3 of drift on a nine-line order**.
The list's whole purpose is that it can be checked; a list that visibly fails to
add is worse than no list.

**So money inside a disclosure renders exact, through `acMoney`.** The rule was
already in the codebase and this simply stops being inconsistent with it —
`public/retail-admin/01-core.js`: *"anywhere an operator might reconcile the
number against something — a list, a total, a dialog, an export — uses acMoney
and shows the real amount."* The unit price already followed it; the amount
beside it did not.

**THE BOUNDARY IS THE BREAKDOWN LINE.** Revenue, both cost rows, operating
expenses, net and every line of the breakdown stay whole yuan — those are §36's
figures and §36's decision, and the fen on `¥37,942` is noise. Only what opens
BELOW a breakdown line renders to the fen, because that is the only place a
reader is doing arithmetic.

**A NOTE ON HOW THIS WAS FOUND, because it is the lesson.** Every test passed,
end-to-end reconciliation passed, and the endpoint's own guarantee — the rows
total the posted figure — was true the whole time and still is. **The defect was
never in the money; it was in the rendering of it**, and no assertion looked at
what two levels of the card said *next to each other*. The suite now renders the
real case and adds the displayed figures up.

#### Still no new Chinese

Third time. The three state sentences are the pairs already live on the two
levels above. The item name is **two columns picked by the reader's language with
a fallback across** — the house pattern for bilingual DATA (`tmStoreLabel` on
stores) and explicitly NOT `finCatLabel`, which splits one glued free-text value.
A category is such a value; an item name is not.


## §89 — MONEY IN IS LISTED FROM THE BEGINNING AND SUMMED FROM 1 AUGUST 2026

**DECIDED 2026-09-10 by Ash, under an explicit delegation given in session:
*"do whatever you think its right"*, after the measurements below were put to
them.** It is recorded that way rather than as a session's own ruling because
this file's authority rule is not something a session may quietly assume; and it
is recorded as a decision rather than a proposal because Ash was asked and
answered. Anyone may overturn it — the numbers it rests on are all here.

### What §55 left open, and why it could not be closed by reading the tree

§55 records a collision it deliberately did not resolve. §36's *Settlement
receipts are excluded from Finance entirely* gives a platform payout no place on
the staircase; §55 puts `income_entries` on the staircase as a summand; and the
live table holds month-end per-channel totals that answer to both descriptions.
§55 ends: *a ruling from Ash is owed before the money-in row is summed.*

**THE FIGURE §55 NAMES COUNTS TWO ROWS OF ELEVEN.** It says ¥151,895.69, which is
the two Mini App rows. Reading the live ledger for 1 June – 31 July 2026 finds
the same shape eleven times — description exactly `6月` or `7月`, category a
channel, dated the last day of the month:

| channel | 30 Jun | 31 Jul |
|---|---|---|
| Mini App 小程序 | 76,105.69 | 75,790.00 |
| Meituan-Yuexiu 美团-越秀 | 16,026.67 | 13,596.89 |
| Gzgrocery 进口超市 | 12,918.40 | 8,875.30 |
| Meituan-Tianhe 美团-天河 | 9,407.25 | — |
| Eleme-Yuexiu 饿了么-越秀 | 2,231.30 | 2,969.72 |
| Eleme-Tianhe 饿了么-天河 | 1,450.76 | — |
| Manual Order 人工订单 | — | 5,219.70 |

**Eleven rows, ¥224,591.68.** The other nine were never counted. This is
CLAUDE.md's rule — a finding filed as a coordinate is where it was found and not
the extent of the problem — arriving on a money figure, and it is the reason the
correction is recorded here rather than folded silently into the ruling.

The whole table is 26 rows, ¥239,841.06, 13 June to 31 July 2026 and nothing
after. Of the ¥15,249.38 that is not a month-end row, roughly ¥14,992 is
individual channel or payment-method takings (`Alipay`, `WeChat- Office`,
`美团团购`, `拼多多`, `Micromarrt`) and **about ¥257 is genuinely non-sale
income** — cardboard recycling, a returned water-bottle deposit, a rider
cancellation penalty. **This table was not "other income that picked up some
settlement rows". It was the shop's monthly sales ledger before the order record
took over.**

### The measurement that decided it

`scripts/diagnose_income_ledger_overlap.js`, run read-only against production on
2026-09-10, compared the ledger against `retail_orders` using the Summary's own
`PAID` filter and day expression:

| month | order record | ledger month-end rows | ledger ÷ orders |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-06 | 169 orders, ¥38,767.35 | ¥118,140.07 | **3.05×** |
| 2026-07 | 445 orders, ¥74,825.44 | ¥106,451.61 | **1.42×** |
| 2026-08 | 584 orders, ¥123,384.02 | — (ledger stopped) | — |
| 2026-09 | 176 orders, ¥35,615.68 | — | — |

Per channel the shape is unmistakable. June: Gzgrocery ¥1,100.50 recorded against
¥12,918.40 actual, Meituan ¥2,669.90 against ¥25,433.92, Mini App ¥34,996.95
against ¥76,105.69. July: Meituan ¥17,662.40 against ¥13,596.89 and Gzgrocery
¥9,422.30 against ¥8,875.30 — **the order record now exceeds the ledger, which is
exactly right, because an order total is gross and a payout is net of
commission.**

**SO NEITHER SIMPLE ANSWER WAS TRUE, AND BOTH WERE PROPOSED BEFORE THE
MEASUREMENT.** The rows are not a clean duplicate: excluding them discards
roughly ¥79,000 of real June trading the order record never captured. They are
not the only record either: summing them double-counts most of July, which the
order record does hold. **June and July are a migration in progress, both sources
partial, overlapping by an amount no arithmetic recovers.**

### The ruling

**A DATE FLOOR ON SUMMING, AND ON SUMMING ONLY.**

1. **`income_entries` rows dated before 2026-08-01 contribute ZERO to any
   staircase total, any Net, and any figure the AI is given.** Not because they
   are wrong, but because for that period neither source is complete and the two
   overlap unmeasurably. A total built on them would be confidently wrong, which
   is worse than a total that declines to include them.

2. **THE LIST IS NOT FLOORED, AND §36 IS NOT AMENDED.** *Finance is not floored
   at the cutover date* governs what Transactions DISPLAYS, and it stands
   untouched: widen the range over June or July and all 26 rows are there, as
   they are today. **A floor on a summand and a floor on a list are different
   things, and the reason §36 gives for refusing the second — that hiding
   spending to keep a line uniform is less true than showing it — is an argument
   for displaying them, not for adding them up.**

3. **The date is not chosen; it is read off the data.** The ledger's last row is
   31 July 2026 and the order record runs complete from 1 August. The handover
   names its own date, which is also the date *Tacet's Finance begins on 1 August
   2026* already records.

4. **A floored total says so on screen.** A window reaching before the cutover
   must say that money in is not summed for that part and why — the §1.12
   discipline of showing what is known plus one sentence for what is not. **A
   silently reduced total is the failure this ruling exists to prevent**, and it
   would be indistinguishable from the bug it is fixing.

**REJECTED: backfilling `income_entries.channel` to mark the settlement rows.**
The column exists (`schema.sql:266`) and the write path never fills it — all 26
live rows are NULL. Marking them would encode a per-row judgement about which
part of a row's money the order record already holds, and for June that judgement
