is not available at any granularity: the overlap is partial within a single row.
A flag would make an unmeasurable thing look measured.

**REJECTED: deriving the overlap by matching ledger rows to orders.** The ledger
row is one month-end figure per channel; the orders are hundreds of rows, gross
where the ledger is net, and in June mostly absent. There is nothing to match on
and a matcher would be inventing its own answer.

### What this closes and what it does not

**CLOSED: §55's Eleme survey question, and the answer is that revenue is not
short today.** `scripts/diagnose_channel_order_presence.js`, run 2026-09-10,
finds Eleme live in `retail_orders` from 2026-08-31 — 12 orders, ¥1,520.38, 11 of
them in September. **The June/July absence that raised the alarm was a migration
artefact and not a live gap**, which is precisely the distinction that script was
written to make: a channel missing in June is history, the same channel missing
last week is money.

**OPEN, AND NEWLY RAISED BY THAT SAME RUN — the `shop` channel has produced 38
orders and zero revenue.** First order 2026-09-06, last 2026-09-08, **all 38
cancelled, ¥2,065.00 of cancelled value, not one paid.** Every other channel
converts: `wechat` 712 paid against 138 cancelled, `gzgrocery` 418 of 419. A new
channel at a 100% failure rate for three days and then silent is not a Finance
question and is not ruled on here, but it is recorded here because this is where
it was found.

**CLOSED 2026-09-10 — IT WAS TESTING. THE SHOP IS NOT OPEN YET.** Ash, asked
directly. **No sale was lost and there is no defect in the QR door**, and the
paragraph above is left as written per this file's convention so that the reading
and its correction both stay legible.

**RECORDED BECAUSE THE READING WAS CONFIDENT AND WRONG.** Every figure in it is
accurate and the conclusion drawn from them was not: 38 orders, zero paid, a
100% cancel rate and a channel that goes silent are exactly what a broken door
looks like, and exactly what a fortnight of testing before opening looks like.
**Nothing in the database distinguishes them** — no column says a shop has not
opened, and `retail_orders` cannot say whether the person holding the phone was
a customer or a member of staff. The follow-up diagnostic went further into the
mechanism (`lib/inventory.js`'s twenty-minute counter clock, Ash 2026-09-06,
which is what reaped 12 of the 38) and none of that narrowed the question either,
because the mechanism is the same whoever is standing there. **A live-data
reading can establish what happened and cannot always establish what it means;
this one needed a sentence from a person, and the cost of not asking earlier was
a paragraph in this file that read as an incident.**

**ONE THING THE RUN FOUND THAT IS NOT CLOSED BY THIS, AND MATTERS WHEN THE SHOP
DOES OPEN: 23 of the 38 carry NO `cancelled_reason` AND NO CURRENT CODE PATH
WRITES ONE BLANK.** There are five writers of that column — the counter clock
(`lib/inventory.js:1400`), the six-hour stale sweep and the supersede path
(`routes/retail.js:7926`, `:7981`), the customer's own QR cancel
(`routes/shop-menu.js:2696`), and the customer cancel endpoint
(`routes/retail.js:20761`, which falls back to `customer_cancelled` rather than
to blank). None of them can produce an empty reason. Harmless on test rows;
on a trading day it is an order cancelling with nothing saying why.

**OPEN — Meituan fell 97% across the cutover.** 158 paid orders in July, 38 in
August, 5 in September, while `wechat` and `gzgrocery` both grew over the same
period. That may be an ordinary commercial fact and it may be a sync that stopped
working; nothing in this reading distinguishes them, and it is recorded rather
than resolved.

**CLOSED 2026-09-10 — THE YUEXIU STORE IS CLOSED UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE. Ash,
asked directly.** It is an ordinary commercial fact. Meituan intake is healthy:
`diagnose_meituan_intake_stop.js` finds the last Meituan order one day old, and
`meituan_sync_log` / `meituan_sync_queue` both writing within the minute.

**THE 97% IS AN ARTEFACT OF AGGREGATING TWO SHOPS INTO ONE CHANNEL, AND THAT IS
THE PART WORTH KEEPING.** Split by store, the two halves say opposite things:

| month | Tianhe (store 1) | Yuexiu (store 2) |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-06 | 10 orders, ¥964.90 | 11 orders, ¥1,705.00 |
| 2026-07 | 31 orders, ¥3,315.40 | 129 orders, ¥14,347.00 |
| 2026-08 | 39 orders, ¥5,056.20 | — |
| 2026-09 | 5 orders, ¥623.70 | — |

**Tianhe GREW through the month the channel "collapsed".** One shop left and the
other traded on, and the channel line reported the sum as a failure. The control
series did its job — eleme, gzgrocery and wechat kept arriving, which is what
ruled out infrastructure — but it was the PER-STORE split that named the cause,
and a channel-level reading could not have got there at all.

**A STANDING CONSEQUENCE FOR EVERY FINANCE FIGURE THAT CROSSES 1 AUGUST 2026.**
Revenue, any month-on-month comparison, and any chart drawn across that boundary
will show Meituan falling away, and **it is a shop closing rather than trade
declining**. Nothing in `retail_orders` says so — `retail_stores` still carries
`is_active=1` for Yuexiu, because the store is not closed in Tacet, only on the
platform. A reader who does not know that will find a collapse that is not there.

**AND THE SECOND CONFIDENT MISREADING OF THIS RUN, RECORDED BESIDE THE FIRST.**
§89 raised two open items off one diagnostic and both were read as faults; both
were ordinary business facts a sentence from a person settled — a shop not yet
open, and a shop closed for now. The pattern is worth naming: **this database
records what happened and not what was intended, and the difference is where
every wrong reading in this section came from.**

**UNCHANGED: no figure on any screen moves because of this section.**
`routes/finance-summary.js` has never read `income_entries`, so nothing in
production sums these rows today. This ruling binds the code that would have, and
that code has not been written.

### DECIDED 2026-09-10 — §90: a capability to void a posted staff claim

Reported by Ash off the live Transactions screen: a ¥200 "Staff claim" row (the
same row v4.196 fixed the name on) offered no way to undo it. §87 already
refuses to let a claim-posted row be edited or deleted directly — it is a
projection of the claim, and any value typed onto it is lost the next time the
claim is decided — but that refusal left no path back at all once a claim was
approved by mistake, approved for the wrong amount, or turned out to be
somebody else's spending. **THIS SECTION RECORDS THE TWO QUESTIONS ASH DECIDED,
ASKED BEFORE ANY CODE WAS WRITTEN, PER THIS FILE'S OWN RULE.**

**QUESTION ONE — WHAT DOES "CANCEL" DO. DECIDED: VOID THE CLAIM, NOT EDIT-AND-
REPOST.** The claim's status moves to a new terminal state, `voided`, which
`lib/expense-posting.js`'s `postClaim` treats exactly as `rejected` already is
— it deletes the `expense_entries` row and returns null, the same branch §87
built for a rejection reversing an approval. **`voided` IS NOT `rejected`,
DELIBERATELY.** Writing `rejected` over an approved claim would read as though
it was never approved, and would overwrite `decided_by` — the one column that
says who approved it — the moment somebody else reversed that call. Two new
columns, `voided_by` / `voided_at` / `void_note` (schema.sql), carry the
reversal beside the untouched approval record, not in place of it. There is no
path back from `voided`, the same one-way shape `rejected` already has — this
is a correction mechanism, not an "un-void."

Editing the claim's own fields (amount, category, who paid) and letting it
re-post was the alternative on the table and was rejected: it would let a
claim's story change after an approver already read and decided it, which is
the exact defect §87's own header comment names for why editing a *submitted*
claim was never built ("a claim that changed under them after they read it is
the defect the approval step exists to prevent"). Voiding and re-submitting a
fresh, correct claim keeps that guarantee; editing a decided one would not.

**QUESTION TWO — WHO IS AUTHORIZED. DECIDED: A NEW CAPABILITY, `expenses:cancel`,
SEPARATE FROM `expenses:approve`.** Reusing `expenses:approve` was the
alternative and was rejected: an owner may want a bookkeeper who can undo a
mistaken approval without also being able to approve one in the first place —
the same reasoning §87 already gives for why `expenses:approve` is not
`finance:record`. `lib/capabilities.js` registers the key with a `money:
'moves'` marker (it is what removes an already-posted row from the books) and
places it in no floor preset — owner, admin and manager hold it because they
hold everything short of the standard exclusions, and `bookkeeper` is the one
preset that names it explicitly, beside `finance:record` and without
`expenses:approve`. `lib/roles.js`'s `migrateExpenseCancelCap` backfills it onto
existing admin/manager/bookkeeper `tenant_roles` rows — edited or not, for the
reason `migrateKitchenRequestCap` gives at length: nobody can have unticked a
key that did not exist yesterday.

**THE ROUTE: `POST /api/retail-admin/staff-expenses/:id/void`** (routes/staff-
expenses.js), gated by a new `requireCanceller` built the same fail-closed way
`requireApprover` is — the owner always passes, an unresolved capability set
403s rather than falling open, because this reverses money already in the
books. It refuses a claim that is not `approved` (nothing to take back out) and
a claim that is `settled` (the employee has already been paid back outside this
system; voiding would remove the expense from the books while leaving the
payment made) — the same guard `/decide` already enforces, reused rather than
restated. `lib/cap-routes.js` maps the route to `expenses:cancel` ABOVE the
generic `/staff-expenses` prefix, the same ordering guard §87 already relies on
for `/decide`: below the general rule, every submitter's floor-preset
`expenses:submit` would answer for a money-reversing route.

**THE SCREEN: a Void link on the claim's Transactions row** (public/retail-
admin/22-finance.js `finTxRow`), where the row's own comment used to say there
was nothing on the other side worth linking to — that note is amended, not left
standing, now that there is an action to offer. Shown only to `can('expenses:
cancel')` and only while the claim is not yet settled — a control that fails
every time it is pressed is the fault §36 already names for a PO link the
opener cannot serve. The Approvals sub-view's status pill (`finAprPill`) gains
a neutral `Voided · 已作废` state, distinct from `is-no`'s Brick refusal colour:
a voided claim was legitimately approved and later reversed, which is a
different fact from having been refused from the start.

**WHAT THIS DOES NOT BUILD.** No UI surfaces `voided_by` / `voided_at` /
`void_note` beyond the pill's label — the data is kept for accountability, not
yet read back anywhere. Voiding a *rejected* or *submitted* claim is refused
(there is nothing posted to reverse); a submitter who wants to withdraw a claim
still waiting on a decision is the shape `routes/staff-expenses.js`'s own header
comment already reserves for later, and is not this.

### FIXED 2026-09-10 — §90's Void reported success and did nothing: two bugs, found by finally hitting the real route

Reported by Ash off the live Transactions screen, minutes after §90 shipped:
*"once i void it its still here and i can void it again."* Every test §90
shipped with passed — because none of them called the real `/decide` or
`/void` ROUTE over HTTP against the real schema. `scripts/test_staff_expenses.js`
exercises `postClaim` and `readBody` as pure functions against hand-built
fixtures; nothing in the suite booted the actual Express routers. Two bugs were
hiding behind that gap, and either alone would have produced exactly this
symptom.

**BUG ONE — NEITHER ROUTE AWAITED `withTransaction`.** `routes/staff-
expenses.js`'s `/decide` and `/void` handlers were not `async` and called
`withTransaction(db, (tx) => {...})` as a fire-and-forget statement. That looks
harmless with better-sqlite3's synchronous binding, and every other call site
in the codebase does await it — this was the only place that didn't. It is not
harmless: `lib/db-transaction.js`'s `acquire()` serialises outermost
transactions through a promise queue (`st.tail.then(run, run)`), and `.then()`
callbacks always run on a LATER MICROTASK, even against an already-resolved
queue. Unawaited, the code immediately after the call — the activity log, the
`after` read, `res.json(...)` — ran on the SAME tick as the call, before a
single statement inside the transaction had executed. **The HTTP response
reported the claim's PRE-decision state as the result of the decision.** A
throw inside the transaction (see Bug Two) became an unhandled promise
rejection outside the route's own try/catch — never logged by its
`console.error`, never turned into the 500 it should have been.

**BUG TWO — THE DELETE WAS ORDERED BEFORE THE REFERENCE TO IT WAS CLEARED.**
`staff_expenses.expense_id` carries `FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES
expense_entries(id)` (schema.sql). Reversing an approval — §90's void, and the
pre-existing but never-actually-reachable-from-the-UI reject-after-approve path
in `/decide` — calls `lib/expense-posting.js`'s `postClaim`, which `DELETE`s
the posted `expense_entries` row. Both routes read the claim, wrote its new
status, and only cleared `expense_id` to the DELETE's result AFTER calling
`postClaim` — so at the moment of the DELETE, `staff_expenses.expense_id` on
the very row being processed still pointed at the row about to be removed, and
SQLite (`foreign_keys=ON`, `database.js`) refused it: `FOREIGN KEY constraint
failed`. **The unit-level fixture for `postClaim` never caught this because it
declares no `expense_id` column and no such constraint** — it is a plain
in-memory `expense_entries` table with nothing referencing it, standing in for
half the real schema.

**TOGETHER: clicking Void threw the FK error inside the un-awaited
transaction, which surfaced nowhere the route could catch it — the response
Express had already half-sent reported success (or the connection simply
hung, depending on timing), the claim's status never actually changed, and the
ledger row stayed exactly where it was.** Ash saw a claim that could be voided
again because nothing had voided it the first time.

**THE FIX.** Both routes are now `async` and `await withTransaction(...)`.
Both transactions now clear `expense_id = NULL` in the SAME `UPDATE` that
writes the new status, before `postClaim` runs — so the row `postClaim` deletes
is never still referenced when the DELETE executes.

**FOUND BY, AND THE LESSON.** Not by re-reading the diff — by writing
`scripts/test_staff_expenses_transaction_timing.js`, which boots the real
`routes/staff-expenses.js` and `routes/finance-transactions.js` behind a real
HTTP server on tenant 1 (Roots — the one tenant id `lib/tenant-db.js` maps
straight onto the shared `database.js` handle rather than a separate
per-tenant file) and calls `/decide` and `/void` exactly as the browser does.
CLAUDE.md's own rule on citations — "a finding filed as a coordinate is where
it was found, not the extent of the problem" — applies to test coverage too:
a suite that only calls a library function directly can be green while the
route wrapped around it is not, and the two are not the same claim. The new
suite also covers the pre-existing reject-after-approve path in `/decide`,
which shared Bug Two and had never been exercised against the real schema
either — it was unreachable from the UI (the Approvals queue offers Approve/
Reject only while a claim is `submitted`) and so had never been noticed.

### DECIDED 2026-09-10 — §91: the approval queue is brought into line with the rulebook, and Approve stops wearing the AI's colour

Raised by Ash off the live screen, immediately after the queue became visible
for the first time (see the §1.22 note below): *"see if it fits tacet design
rules."* Four things were wrong, three of them mechanical and one a decision.
**Ash decided all four in one instruction — "correct and fix all" — and the
one that is a real choice is recorded here because a later session reading the
button will otherwise see a plain Ink control and "restore" the CTA.**

**THE DECISION — APPROVE IS INK, NOT DUSK.** It shipped as `.fin-cta`, Finance's
Dusk fill. `tacet-desktop-patterns.md` §1.8 refuses that on two counts, and only
the second one settles it:

- **Rule 4, the counting half.** One Dusk CTA per page. This button is per row,
  so a queue of six drew six of them, and the screenshot that started this only
  looked compliant because the tenant had exactly one claim waiting.
- **Rule 5's axis, the half that decides it.** Dusk means one thing — *tacet did
  this for you*. The question is not where the button sits but **who is acting**,
  and an approver deciding a claim is the operator acting, precisely as a modal
  confirm is. That is the same correction that made modal primaries Ink in
  2026-07-26, and the same reasoning that gives Profile zero Dusk. **Having an
  unspent Dusk budget does not convert the merchant's action into the AI's.**

Approve therefore takes the house Ink primary, copied from `.cs-modal
.btn-primary` rather than re-picked, and **keeps its lead over Reject** — the
hierarchy §87 wanted (the queue exists to be cleared; most claims in it are
real) survives, it is simply no longer drawn in a colour that lies. Finance's one
legitimate Dusk element is untouched: `New transaction`, the header CTA that
holds rule 1's first claim. The styling sits on its own `.fin-apr-yes` class
rather than as an override on `.fin-cta`, so that CTA cannot be restyled from
here by someone tidying the rule.

**THE THREE MECHANICAL ONES.** No judgement in any of them; each was the
rulebook already saying so and the code not doing it.

1. **§1.22 — the blocks were `<section>`s and therefore invisible.** Recorded in
   full at `tacet-desktop-patterns.md` §1.22 as the fourth bite. The first fix
   shipped (PR #474) was `display: block`, which that section explicitly
   forbids; PR #476 replaced it with the tag change it prescribes. **The blocks
   move, never the rule.**
2. **§1.13a rule 3 — the band read `--td-raised`, not `--td-header`**, while the
   comment directly above it named the right token. Raised is the surface the
   card already sits on, so the band and the rows differed by nothing.
   `--td-header` exists because exactly that comparison was made and rejected.
   The band also now pins (rule 1), which required swapping the card's
   `overflow: hidden` for `clip-path: inset(0 round 14px)` — rule 2's mechanism,
   because `overflow` would make the card the scrollport and park the band on
   row one.
3. **§1.6 — the column headers rendered `DATE / ASKED BY / AMOUNT`.** The markup
   emits sentence case and Finance's own rule declares 13px/500 Ink; the global
   `th` rule supplies `uppercase` + `.08em`, and **specificity is compared per
   property**, so a property Finance never declared had exactly one candidate in
   the cascade. Same shape as §1.22, one property over. Both properties are now
   declared explicitly, with a note saying why they cannot be tidied away.

**NOT CHANGED, AND CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED.** The `Voided` pill is neutral
(`--td-raised` + border), which looked at first like a §1.10 miss because that
table files "cancelled" under Brick. It is correct: §1.10's own receipts define
neutral treatment as exactly this, and §90 distinguishes a reversal from a
refusal on purpose — painting both Brick would collapse two states the product
deliberately separates. **The dates were also checked and are right**: `tdWhen`
applies §1.18's conditional-year rule in the store's timezone, so a claim from
last year renders `Dec 14, 2025` on a queue that has no window. Neither needed a
change and both are written down here so the next pass does not re-open them.

**THE RANGE ECHO, which is the one nobody had noticed.** §87 hides the range bar
on this sub-view and on Categories, and says why: a queue is waiting *now*, and a
bar reading "30 days" over it would suggest there are older claims it is hiding.
The bar was hidden. **The echo in the page head was not**, so the queue sat under
`Aug 12 – Sep 10 · 30 days` — the exact claim the bar was hidden to prevent, and
now unanswerable, because the control that would have changed it was gone. Both
elements say one thing and only one of them had been told. §1.17: a page may not
claim something that is not true of what is under it.

**GUARDED, NOT JUST FIXED.** `scripts/test_finance_approvals.js` gains four
assertions — the blocks are divs and no `display` override has come back, the
band is Ink on `--td-header` and sentence case and pinned, Approve carries no
`.fin-cta` and no `--td-dusk`, and the echo leaves with the bar. Every one of
these is a thing a later edit could quietly undo, which is what that suite is
for.

## §92 — THE LEDGER ROW SAYS WHO PUT IT IN THE BOOKS

**DECIDED 2026-09-10 by Ash**, off the live Transactions screen, against the
¥200 `Asher · personal` row: *"why it doesn't show the user name that post
this?"*

### The confusion is real and it is between two different people

§87 put the SPENDER in the description. `Asher · personal` is who spent the
money and the note they typed, and v4.190's reasoning for putting it there
stands: a ¥38 line with no supplier, no invoice and no purchase order behind it
is answerable months later only if it says whose taxi it was.

`created_by` is the other fact. It has meant *who put this row in the books*
since `expense_entries` existed, and `lib/expense-posting.js` writes the
approver's `decided_by` into it on purpose — "who spent it is in the description
and on the claim".

**On a claim row those are two different people doing two different things, and
the screen showed one of them.** An operator reading a name beside `Staff claim`
has no way to tell which one they are looking at.

### Both facts were already stored; one had never been read

Nothing was missing from the database. `routes/finance-transactions.js` selected
`description` and not `created_by`, so the payload carried no such field and the
screen had nowhere to draw one. The CSV's `Entered by` column named a MECHANISM
— `Purchasing`, `Staff claim`, `Entered by hand` — and never a person.

**So this is a recorded fact reaching a reader, not a new fact being recorded.**
That is why there is no migration, no new column, and why the answer is true of
every row already in the books.

### Read-time, which v4.196 rejected for the other name

v4.196 rejected resolving a name at read time in this exact file, and recorded
why: v4.190 had placed the SPENDER in the description where the poster snapshots
it, so resolving it again at read would print it twice. It also recorded that
read-time is "the more robust mechanism — it reaches every existing row and
follows a later rename".

**Neither objection reaches the approver.** Nothing snapshots it, so there is
nothing to print twice; and read-time is what makes the answer true of the rows
Ash was looking at when he asked, rather than only of rows written afterwards.

**REJECTED: a `created_by_name` snapshot column**, the shape `material_requests`
already uses. It needs a migration to buy a worse answer — it would name nobody
on every row currently in the books, which is every row in the question.

### Two labels, because they are two acts

| row | label |
|---|---|
| posted by an approved claim | `Approved by` · `审批人` |
| typed by hand, either direction | `Entered by` · `录入人` |
| posted by Purchasing | *unnamed — keeps `Posted by Purchasing`* |

Approving somebody else's spending is an exercise of authority §87 built a
capability around; typing a row is not. **One label over both would flatten an
approval into a piece of typing.**

**A PO ROW IS NOT NAMED, and that is not an oversight.** One PO row on this
screen is a collapse of several `expense_entries` rows whose posters can differ,
so naming it means picking one arbitrarily. `Posted by Purchasing` is the true
answer for a row nobody typed, and the CSV cell is empty for the same reason.

**A NAME THAT DOES NOT RESOLVE RENDERS NOTHING.** §1.12 prefers an empty cell to
an invented one. The live `Someone · 未知` belongs to the approvals queue, where
the name is the whole purpose of the column it sits in; on a ledger row it would
be noise asserting an absence.

### The lookup is one FILE now, which is v4.196's argument applied twice

v4.196 made one function out of two lookups because "a second lookup shaped
slightly differently is the whole mechanism by which they would" drift — the
name on the approver's screen and the name in the books must agree. **A third
reader in a second route file means one function is no longer enough.**
`lib/user-names.js` is the one place a `tenant_users` id becomes a name;
`routes/staff-expenses.js` delegates to it and keeps `submitterNames` as its
local name.

**THE CROSS-HANDLE READ DID NOT WEAKEN A TEST TO GET THERE.**
`scripts/test_finance_transactions.js` forbids `require('../database')` in
`routes/finance-transactions.js`, because `routes/finance.js` reads TENANT data
off the global handle and is the pattern that assertion exists to keep out.
`tenant_users` is control-plane and has nowhere else to come from — a real
distinction — so the read went into a lib that names it, and the suite now also
asserts that the route STILL never requires `../database` and that the lib never
reads a tenant table. **Relaxing the assertion instead would have been the edit
that makes the next real instance invisible.**

**ONE READ FOR THE WHOLE PAGE.** The ids are collected across all three lists
before the list is built. A per-row lookup over a 2,000-row window is 2,000
cross-handle queries to print a handful of distinct names.

### What is deliberately not done

**The breakdown's third-level rows (`finCatRow`) are not given the name.** That
surface is a dense figure inside an opened category, not the ledger an operator
works, and the row there is already carrying a date, a name and a mark. Recorded
so a later reader finds a decision rather than an omission.

## §93 — THE COUNTER TAKES POINTS AND WALLET BALANCE, AND THE TILL IS THE COUNTER PATH

**Decided by Ash, 2026-09-10**, from the question that opened the session: *"whats the different between counter till and new order button in orders page? maybe better remove the new order button and just use the till with some extra improvment that we need already anyway, like pay with points, banace etc..."*

**THE TWO ARE NOT DUPLICATES AND ONE OF THEM IS NOT GOING AWAY.** The proposal was surveyed before it was answered. `public/till.html` is a cashier screen: one store, tap-to-add, settle, and every sale it writes is already paid, `fulfillment_type: 'counter'`, `channel: 'shop'`, `shop_entry_method: 'till'`. The New order page (`#tab-orders-new`) is an order-authoring page: delivery addresses with zone-driven fees, unpaid orders with a pay link, wholesale, drafts, customer and staff notes, a grand-total override. The till has none of those and should not grow them — a tablet at a counter is the wrong place to key a wholesale delivery. **Removing New order would have removed the ability to take a phone order.** So the overlap is narrowed rather than the page deleted, and the overlap is exactly one row: New order's Fulfilment = "Counter sale". That half is §93's second change and ships separately.

**WHAT WAS ACTUALLY WRONG WAS THE THING THE PROPOSAL ASKED FOR.** `POST /api/retail-admin/orders` has listed `'points'` and `'balance'` in `ALLOWED_PAY` since the off-app tenders landed, **and touched neither ledger**. An order could be filed as paid in points with the customer's `points_balance` untouched — and `markOrderPaid` would then call `awardOrderPoints` and hand them MORE points for the privilege. **It had never happened, and only because no screen offered the values**: `PAY_METHOD_CHOICES` is the five off-app wallets and the New order form's select is offline/wechat/alipay/other. The hole was latent, not live, which is the only reason this is a feature rather than an incident. **The words on the row are now true**, which is the smallest correct description of this change.

**THE RULE IS THE CHECKOUT'S RULE, LIFTED, NOT A SECOND ONE WRITTEN FOR THE COUNTER.** `manualOrderCredit` calls `pointsRedeemableBase`, `pointsRequiredFor`, `pointsCashValue`, `walletSpendForOrder` and `sweepExpiredPoints` — the same functions `POST /api/retail/orders` redeems through — and applies them in the same order: **points first, then balance, because points expire and a wallet does not**, so spending the perishable tender first is what costs the customer least. A shop that changes `points.redeemRate` changes both surfaces at once, which is the whole reason the helper reads the setting rather than the till doing the arithmetic.

**`points_to_use` IS A REQUEST, NOT AN INSTRUCTION, and the distinction is load-bearing.** The till sends the WHOLE of the customer's balance and lets the server clamp it to what the order can absorb, because the clamp depends on `points.redeemRate` and `points.coverShipping` — settings the till would otherwise re-implement and be wrong about on the day one of them changed. **Asking for more points than the customer HAS is a different thing and is refused rather than clamped**: it means the screen was showing a stale balance, and quietly charging the difference to the card is exactly the failure the checkout's own `insufficient_points` exists to prevent.

**TWO CEILINGS, AND THE SECOND ONE IS NEW.** The shop's redeemable base is the first, as at checkout. The second is **the bill actually due**, and it exists because this route has something the checkout does not: a grand-total override. Without it an order overridden down to ¥5 would still redeem against the ¥50 of goods behind it, and the shop would hand back ¥45 of credit it never charged for. **Balance is capped a third time, at the bill less shipping, and that one is not a setting**: store credit never pays a shipping fee and there is no switch that lets it (`walletSpendableBase`). Points pay shipping only where `points.coverShipping` says so, which is off by default.

**CREDIT IS DECIDED BEFORE THE TRANSACTION AND SPENT INSIDE IT.** The two balance reads do not belong inside a write lock, and the deduction does — against the same conditional `UPDATE`s the checkout uses, so the floor check and the write are one statement and two tills settling the same customer at once cannot both read ¥40 and both spend it. **A failed floor check throws rather than clamping**: the order row is already in that transaction, unwinding costs nothing, and clamping would let a customer walk out having paid a residual computed against credit that was not there. It leaves as a **409 with the same code the checkout answers**, so a client has one case to handle. **The customer whose credit is spent is the one resolved BEFORE the transaction opens, never one minted inside it** — a guest-with-save has no points to spend and is refused by name (`credit_requires_customer`) rather than charged in full as though the credit had applied.

**THE TENDERS ARE STORED BESIDE THE CASH, NOT FOLDED INTO IT.** `points_used`, `points_amount` and `balance_used` go on the order row, so `orderTenders` and `splitRefundAcrossTenders` — which already existed and already knew how to divide a refund three ways — return each refunded ¥ to where it came from. **Folding the credit into `total` would have made every refund all-cash**, returning money the shop never took.

**AT THE TILL, THE CREDIT IS TWO CHECKBOXES AND NOT A SLIDER.** A cashier at a counter spends the points or does not; a partial redemption is a decision nobody makes standing at a till with a queue behind them. **Both are OFF on every sale** — defaulting to "spend everything" would burn a balance somebody was saving, silently, one tap from done — and they clear with the customer they belong to, on removal, on swap and on reset. **The indicator is a square where the wallet rows are circles**, because points and balance are independent and the wallets are a radio group: a round indicator on a multi-select is the one place this screen would be lying about how it behaves. **The row carries its own figure**, since "how much does this take off?" is the question being asked and the wallets' one big number cannot answer it.

**THE WALLET PICKER DISAPPEARS WHEN THERE IS NOTHING LEFT TO TAKE, and the counter-sale wallet rule is NARROWED RATHER THAN BROKEN.** That rule — a walk-in must name the wallet that took the money — exists because an off-app sale reconciles against a terminal's daily statement and `'offline'` reconciles against nothing. **Credit covering the bill in full means no terminal was touched**, so asking which wallet took it would be asking the cashier to invent a reconciliation. The order still names its tender: `'points'`, or `'balance'` when the wallet did it alone. **Every ¥ of CASH still names the wallet that took it**, unchanged.

**THE DONE SCREEN PRINTS THE SALE, NOT THE CASH.** `total` after credit is the residual, and on a bill settled entirely in points that is ¥0.00 — a figure that reads as a giveaway. The headline is the sum of the three tenders, which is `orderTenders`' own definition of the gross, so the counter and the server agree on what the sale was worth. **And a wallet is named only if a wallet took something**: a cashier who picks WeChat and then applies enough credit to cover the bill leaves `S.wallet` set behind them, and printing it would put a tender on a receipt for money that terminal never saw.

**NOT OFFERED ON A RECALLED QR ORDER, and that is a property of the settle path rather than of the screen.** A recall `PATCH`es the existing row's status and nothing else, so credit chosen there would be shown, charged as though it applied, and never deducted. The customer already picked their tender on their own phone. Making it work needs the redemption to move to the status transition, which is a different change; **a control that silently does nothing is worse than no control.**

**THE TILL MINTS NOTHING; THE TWO ERROR CATALOGUES DO, AND FOUR PAIRS ARE DECLARED.** The credit rows carry `points` and `wallet`, already locked in this file's own `STRINGS`; the gross on the settle subline is its own `total`; every other value on a row is a numeral or a currency figure, and a numeral takes no label. That is §30 rule 3's preference — restructure the label so a live string fits rather than mint one — applied rather than quoted, and the counter screen owes nothing.

**What was not foreseen is that the SERVER's new refusals do.** Both order forms — the desktop's and the phone's — are gated by suites requiring every code the endpoint can answer with to have a slot and a sentence, and the four new codes tripped both. **Neither form can actually cause them** (neither sends `points_to_use` or `use_balance`; the till does), and they are written anyway for the reason §44's three door codes were: a code with no home lands at the top of the form rather than beside the control that caused it. **Two of the four are quoted, not composed** — `insufficient_points` from the admin's own shared catalogue, `insufficient_balance` from the pair the storefront and the mini app both already ship for it. **Two are composed** under Rule 4's standing delegation, from words checked live in the tree rather than assumed, and are declared in `docs/tacet-delivery-vocabulary.md` with the candidates rejected — including `未付清`, which is the natural phrase and appears in zero files. They exist because **no screen in this product has ever had to say that a tender fell short of the bill**: until §93 no hand-keyed order had a tender that could.

**One thing was got wrong on the way and is recorded because the file itself warns about it:** two new comments in `till.html` quoted Chinese characters to illustrate what a row renders, which the house rule at `renderCust` forbids **for comments too** — "a character that never renders is still one nobody checked against a source". Both were rewritten to name the string keys instead.

**HELD BY A SUITE THAT WAS PROVEN ABLE TO GO RED, IN BOTH ITS HALVES.** `scripts/test_till_credit.js` (fast shard) exercises `manualOrderCredit` directly and then **lifts the real route handler and drives it** over a real schema with the real transaction helper — so what is asserted is that a sale actually moves the balances, writes the two ledger rows, charges the residual, and that a refusal writes nothing at all. `TC_MUTANT=1` restores the pre-fix behaviour. **The mutation is a function rather than a one-off because this file lifts the helper TWICE**: mutating only the first lift left eleven end-to-end assertions passing against a helper that returned nothing, which is the "green over nothing" this record has twice caught elsewhere (v4.196, v4.154). **And the first mutation guard was anchored on the points read, which `sweepExpiredPoints` also makes** — so it fired on a function the mutation had not touched and reported a mutation that HAD taken as failed. A guard that fires on the wrong function is worse than none.

**ONE ASSERTION WAS RE-SCOPED, NOT RELAXED, AND IT NOW PROVES MORE.** `verify-fulfilment-types.js` pinned the literal source of the till's settle gate — `ready: function (st) { return !!st.wallet; }` — and went red for a change that made the rule more careful. That is the rot its own runner's header warns about. The function is now **lifted and executed** against stubbed money, holding the behaviour in four rows: cash refuses without a wallet, cash confirms with one, a fully covered bill needs none, **and a zero bill with no credit behind it still refuses** — the escape being the credit, not the zero. A `ready` that simply returned true satisfies no row.

**`test_tax.js` AND `test_tx_conversion_manual_order.js` LIFT THE REAL HELPER, NOT A STUB.** Both drive this handler and both needed it in scope. A stub returning zero would have taken the credit back out of the very things those files measure — what the create route stores, and what commits together — so the real chain is lifted into both. No case in either asks for credit, so every existing assertion is answered exactly as before; what is bought is that the day one does, those files notice.

### Open items

- **The counter-sale row leaves the New order form.** The page can still be set to Fulfilment = "Counter sale", and while it can it writes a **mis-attributed row**: `channel: 'shop'` requires `shop_entry_method`, the form offers neither, so a counter sale keyed in the back office files as pickup or other and **falls outside the shop's revenue line** that §44's amendment exists to keep whole. That is the second half of Ash's decision and ships as its own PR.
- **A recalled QR order cannot spend credit** (above). Reachable only by moving the redemption to the status transition.
- **Partial points** — spending some of a balance rather than all of it — is deliberately not offered at the counter. The server already accepts any figure in `points_to_use`, so a later screen needs no server change.


## §94 — THE NEW ORDER FORM STOPS OFFERING A COUNTER SALE

**Decided by Ash, 2026-09-10**, as the second half of §93. The original question was whether the New order button could go away entirely in favour of the till; §93 answered no, and recorded that the two surfaces overlap in exactly one row. **This removes that row.**

**IT COULD NOT PRODUCE A CORRECT ROW, AND HAD NOT SINCE §44 WAS AMENDED.** A shop sale is `channel: 'shop'` carrying a `shop_entry_method` that names the door — till or QR — and the server enforces both halves symmetrically: a 'shop' order MUST name its door, and any other channel must NOT. **This form sends neither.** It offers no 'shop' origin, deliberately and correctly, because a shop sale is not an answer to *"how did the customer reach us?"*; and having no origin, it has no door to name. So a walk-in keyed on this page filed as `pickup` or `other` and **fell out of the shop's revenue line**, which is the one thing §44's amendment exists to keep whole.

**THE DEFECT WAS SILENT, which is why it survived.** The order was created, the stock moved, the money was recorded and the receipt printed. Only the attribution was wrong, and attribution is the thing nobody checks until the month's figures do not match the shop's own sense of its day.

**THE PHONE HAS ONLY EVER OFFERED TWO.** `ONW_FULS` in `public/m.html` is delivery and pickup and always has been. This is the desktop catching up with a choice already made on the other copy of the same form, not a new rule — and the two surfaces now agree, which they did not before.

**WHAT IS NOT CHANGED, and the distinction is the whole of the risk here.** `counter` remains a server fulfilment type. The till goes on writing it, `lib/fulfilment` goes on branching on it, `isTerminalOnPaid` goes on flipping it to its terminal state, and **every counter error code keeps its slot and its sentence in both forms' catalogues** — `store_required_for_counter`, `payment_method_required_for_counter`, `address_not_allowed_for_counter`, `shipping_fee_not_allowed_for_counter`, `pos_closed_for_store`. The endpoint can still answer with all of them, to the till, and a code the server can send with no home on the page is what those catalogues exist to prevent. **This is a change to one picker, not to what a counter sale is.**

**TWO BRANCHES ARE DELETED RATHER THAN LEFT STANDING.** `ordNewFulChange` opened a counter sale on Paid · Cash and put the pending defaults back on the way out; `ordNewPaintFeeNote` had a sentence for it. Neither had any way of being reached once the option and the draft path were closed. **An unreachable branch reads as a rule this form still has**, and the next person to read it would have to work out that it does not.

**AN OLD DRAFT SAVED AS A COUNTER SALE COMES BACK AS A PICKUP.** This is the one behaviour an operator can actually walk into, and it needed a decision rather than a default. Setting a `<select>` to a value it has no option for leaves it on whatever was already selected — so a counter draft would have restored as a **DELIVERY**, silently acquiring an address requirement it was never written with, and refusing to save until the operator filled in six fields for a walk-in. **Pickup is the honest neighbour**: nothing ships, the customer collects at a store, and the address block stays absent exactly as it was when the draft was saved. The status and pay method the operator had chosen are restored on top, untouched. **The draft's stored payload is NOT rewritten** — this is a reading of an old draft, not an edit to one.

**NO CHINESE IS MINTED OR TOUCHED.** The option's own locked pair leaves with the option; every counter sentence in both catalogues stays exactly as it is, because the till can still cause every one of them. **No entry in `docs/tacet-delivery-vocabulary.md` is owed.**

**NO SIGNPOST WAS ADDED, and that is a decision rather than an omission.** The obvious kindness is a caption under the picker pointing at the till. It would have had to carry two bilingual pairs — `Counter sale · 前台销售` and `Counter till · 前台收银` — inside one element, and a single element holding two `EN · CN` pairs is precisely the shape the DOM-walker cannot read and `check-i18n-banners.js` exists to refuse. Composing a fresh sentence to avoid that would mint a string to explain the absence of a control, which is the wrong trade. **The till is already a rail row on this screen** (its own §, added because a tool nobody can find is a tool nobody has), so the path is one click away and named.

**FOUR ASSERTIONS WERE RE-SCOPED, NOT RELAXED, AND THE REPLACEMENTS WERE PROVEN RED — by reverting both files and re-running, not by assuming.** The counter-defaults assertion is replaced by three that hold more than it did: the picker offers exactly delivery and pickup and nothing else; neither remaining fulfilment writes the status or the pay method; and `counter` is still a server type, asserted through `lib/fulfilment` itself rather than through a list typed into the test. The address-block and hand-picked-fulfilment rows drop their counter case, the latter keeping the case that still exists — a hand-picked Pickup surviving the origin that would otherwise have set it.

**THE DRAFT MAP IS EVALUATED, NOT DESCRIBED.** The mapping expression is lifted out of `ordNewRestore` and run over all three inputs. The wiring around it is read rather than run, and the reason is recorded: `ordNewRestore` drives a dozen DOM nodes and two async pickers, and a harness for it would be testing the stubs. What the source is held to is the property that actually matters — **no read of the raw stored fulfilment survives outside that one expression**, which is exactly how this bug would come back. It is counted with the mapping line removed rather than as a total, so a harmless rewrite of the expression does not go red for the wrong reason.

### Open items

- **A recalled QR order still cannot spend store credit** (§93). Unchanged by this.
- **Nothing back-fills the rows already written.** Counter sales keyed on this form before today carry `pickup` or `other` and sit outside the shop's revenue line. How many there are is not known and is worth measuring before deciding whether a repair is worth writing; a migration that guesses which past `pickup` orders were really walk-ins would be inventing attribution, not restoring it.


## §95 — A CUSTOMER ROW HAS ONE SHAPE, AND THE TILL NORMALISES IT AT THE BOUNDARY

**Reported by Ash, 2026-09-10**, from the till's customer picker, within an hour of §93 going live: *"it doesnt show points, everyone at 0, only wallet amount work."*

**THE CAUSE WAS A FIELD NAME.** `/api/retail-admin/customers` returns its `SELECT` verbatim, so every row carries `points_balance` — the column's name — while the wallet's column is simply `balance`. `public/till.html` read `c.points`, which no row has ever had. One of the two was spelled the way the file guessed and one was not, which is precisely why the symptom looked like a points problem rather than a naming one.

**IT WAS COSMETIC FOR AS LONG AS THE TILL ONLY DISPLAYED IT, AND STOPPED BEING COSMETIC AT §93.** That change gave the counter something to spend, and `creditOffer` reads the same field: `pMax` was zero for every customer alive, the points control never drew, and **the headline half of what had shipped an hour earlier could not be reached at all.** The wallet worked throughout — which is what made the report so exact, and what would have made this very hard to find from a vaguer one.

**NORMALISED AT THE BOUNDARY, NOT AT THE READERS.** `custRow()` maps a row once, at the single place rows enter this screen, and the four readers are left alone. Patching each reader was the smaller diff and **is the reason the bug existed in the first place**: knowing the trick was the requirement, so the fifth reader would have had to know it too. Both spellings are accepted, so the shape does not depend on which endpoint a later caller reaches for, and both are coerced to numbers so the call sites have nothing left to defend against.

**THE SERVER IS NOT TOUCHED, and that is a decision.** Aliasing the column to `points` in the endpoint would have fixed this screen and changed the shape under every other reader of that route — the customers roster, the mobile list, anything written since. The client that guessed is the client that should stop guessing.

### Why the suite that shipped alongside it did not catch this

**This is the part worth keeping.** `test_till_credit.js` shipped with §93 carrying forty assertions — the redemption arithmetic, the route's wiring, the transaction boundary, both ledger rows, the till's payload and its reset paths — and **every one of them passed against a feature that could not be used**.

**Each assertion built its own customer object, and each spelled the field the way the code under test spelled it.** The suite and the bug shared an assumption, so the suite could not see it. A test that invents its input cannot catch an input invented wrongly, and no amount of adding assertions of the same kind would have helped.

The three that replace that gap do not invent an input:

- the endpoint's own `SELECT` is **read** for the field name, so a later rename fails here rather than in front of a cashier;
- `custRow` is **run** against a row shaped like the endpoint's;
- `creditOffer` is **run** against the result — and against a companion row deliberately left un-normalised, so the fixture stops proving anything the moment the boundary stops mattering.

All three were **proven red against the shipped file**, by checking it out and re-running, not by assuming.

### Open items

- **Nothing else was audited for the same class of guess.** This screen was fixed because it was reported. Other clients reading that route may spell the same column the same wrong way, and the endpoint returning raw column names means the question is open wherever a reader was written from memory rather than from the response. Worth a sweep; not done here, because a sweep is a different change from a fix.


## §96 — THE CUSTOMER-LIST SWEEP: CLEAN, AND THE TWO RENAMERS ARE PINNED

**Asked for by Ash, 2026-09-10**, on the open item §95 left behind: other clients reading `/api/retail-admin/customers` might spell its columns the same wrong way the till did.

**THEY DO NOT. The sweep is clean.** Every caller of that route was read:

| caller | how it reads the row | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `08-customers.js` — the desktop roster | `points_balance`, `lifetime_spend`, `tier_key`, `orders_count`, `is_blocked`, `balance` | raw columns, correct |
| `02-settings-ops.js` — global search | `nickname`, `phone`, `orders_count` | correct |
| `04-orders.js` — New order picker | `nickname`, `phone`, `orders_count` | correct |
| `24-import.js` — the importer | `id`, `phone`, `nickname`, `note`, `tags` | correct |
| `05-marketing.js` — grant search | `nickname`, `phone`, `openid` | correct |
| `m.html` — phone back office | maps `points_balance` → `points`, `balance` → `wallet` at the boundary | correct, and now pinned |
| `till.html` | read `c.points` | **the §95 bug, fixed** |

The other two customer routes are clean for reasons of their own. `by-phone` returns `is_blocked` and `nickname` and its reader uses exactly those. **`store-admin`'s lookup camel-cases on the SERVER** — `pointsBalance`, `lifetimeSpend`, `isBlocked` — so its client is handed a shape rather than guessing one.

**A NEGATIVE RESULT IS THE FINDING, and it is written down rather than left as a silence.** "Nobody swept" and "somebody swept and it was clean" are different states, and only one of them saves the next person the work.

### The one guard, and why it is the whole of the change

**Exactly two clients rename this endpoint's columns**: the till's `custRow`, added by §95, and the phone back office's mapper. **The phone's has been right all along and had nothing holding it there** — which is precisely the standing §95's own subject had on the morning it shipped broken. Two clients renaming one endpoint's field is two chances to drift, and the endpoint is the thing both must follow. Both are now pinned to it, in one place, beside the contract assertion §95 added. **Proven red by breaking the phone mapper and re-running**, not assumed.

### Rejected

- **Rejected: aliasing the column to `points` in the endpoint.** It would remove the need for either normaliser — and change the shape under all five readers that are correct today. It fixes nothing that is broken and puts five working screens at risk to tidy two that are not.
- **Rejected: a general lint holding that no client may read a field its endpoint does not send.** The rule is right; the mechanism is not available. These routes build their `SELECT`s from interpolated fragments, so the returned shape is not statically knowable, and a checker that guessed it would be wrong exactly where the guessing is hardest. **Two named pins that are exact beat one general rule that is approximate** — and the general rule, being approximate, would have had to be allowed to pass things it could not parse, which is the shape of a check that proves nothing.
- **Rejected: widening the sweep to every endpoint in the product.** The question asked was about customer rows, the answer is now known, and an audit of two hundred routes is a different piece of work that should be chosen deliberately rather than arrived at.

## §97 — THE PHONE MATCHES THE PC. THE "DELIBERATELY NOT THE DESKTOP" RULE IS RETIRED

**Decided by Ash, 2026-09-10:** *"mobile version functionality should be the same as PC."* Page by page, starting with Orders.

**This overrides a rule that is written down and was, until today, correct.** `docs/tacet-mobile-parity.md` §"How the two surfaces differ by design" says: *"The phone is deliberately not the desktop … What the phone owes an operator is the daily loop … So a missing capability is only a defect when it is part of that loop. Each row below is judged on that, not on 'the desktop has it.'"* That sentence is why roughly thirty rows in that document are `➖` rather than bugs, and it is why the 2026-08-22 audit could close with Orders marked done.

**It is retired, not deleted.** The old document is not rewritten — every `➖` in it stays where it is, and so does the reason beside it. What changes is how those rows are READ: a `➖` is now an open gap with an argument attached, and the argument is Ash's to overrule rather than a session's to inherit. **Anyone re-reading that document must read this section first.**

### Why the old rule is worth retiring rather than defending

It was not wrong when it was written; it stopped matching what the phone had become. Two of its own `➖` reasons had already expired by the time anyone re-read them (`docs/tacet-mobile-orders-parity-survey.md` §3) — the staff note was blocked on a backend endpoint that now exists. **A rule whose exceptions rot is a rule that has to be re-checked to be used, and nobody was re-checking it.** "The phone does what the PC does" needs no per-row judgement and cannot go stale.

### What "the same as PC" means, precisely

**The same CAPABILITIES, not the same LAYOUT.** A phone renders a sheet where the desktop renders a drawer; a phone asks with a bottom sheet where the desktop opens a modal. None of that is in scope. What is in scope is the answer to *"can an operator do this thing at all from a phone?"* — and after this section the answer is yes, unless this document says otherwise for a named reason.

**Authoring is no longer an automatic exemption.** "Full authoring on desktop" was a corollary of the retired rule and travels with it. Where authoring stays on the desktop from here, it stays for a reason recorded per case, not because it is authoring.

### The three exceptions, decided with the rule

**Left out for now, and NOT decided as permanent:** the courier map, the Qingyun delivery-point map picker, and the JD label printer. Each is a desktop-shaped integration — two maps you click a point on, and a component that talks to a printer attached to the PC. **A phone version of each needs a phone design before any code**, which is a separate question from parity and should be chosen deliberately rather than arrived at inside a parity sweep. They are open, not closed.

### The order of work, and the standing rule for every step of it

Orders first, as the page Ash named. Within Orders, staged in `docs/tacet-mobile-orders-parity-survey.md` §5 — the refund and cancel half of the status machine first, because it is the only gap on that page that leaves an operator with a customer in front of them and no answer.

**Every write added under this section is asserted on the REQUEST** — the endpoint, the method and every field of the body — not on the toast. That rule is the phone's own, recorded twice in the 2026-08-22 audit after this app shipped a write that reported success and sent nothing, and widening the phone's write surface is exactly when it earns its keep.

**Every guard the desktop puts in front of a write comes with the write.** A confirm the PC asks and the phone does not is not parity with a smaller screen — it is the same button with the safety removed. Named, for Orders: the early-dispatch warning and the cancellation reason.

### Rejected

- **Rejected: fixing the whole of Orders in one change.** The page is twenty-odd missing endpoints and eight list-level features. One PR per group, as `docs/tacet-mobile-orders-parity-survey.md` §5 stages it — a single diff that large cannot be reviewed and cannot be reverted in pieces.
- **Rejected: rewriting `docs/tacet-mobile-parity.md` to remove the retired rule.** It is a dated audit and its findings are true as of their date. Editing a closed audit to match a later decision destroys the record of what was believed when. This section supersedes it in place; the pointer is one-way and forward.
- **Rejected: deciding the three map/printer exceptions permanently, either way.** Neither "port them as they are" nor "desktop forever" can be chosen without a phone design to look at. Recording them as open is the honest state.

## §98 — A LATE PARCEL THAT SPOILED THE FOOD IS A CASE WITH STEPS, AND THE CARRIER'S MONEY IS NOT INCOME UNTIL IT LANDS

**Decided 2026-09-11 by Ash**, asked from the phone and described in their own words: the customer's package arrived complete but late, the fresh items in it were spoiled, the carrier is given evidence and pays for the spoiled goods, and replacement goods go back out to the customer. Ash's framing of the money, which corrects the session's first reading of it: *"jingdong will pay a certain amount for the spoiled products so it doesn't really cost roots … but we do have the cost for the new food that been shipped out."* And on scope: *"maybe other tenants have different configuration, they should be able to do this."*

**Two rulings taken in session.** The replacement leaves as **a second order priced ¥0, linked to the first**. And step three **branches**: sometimes the customer would rather have their money back than another parcel.

### What already exists, and why this is not a new module

Measured 2026-09-11 against main at `5ab75c8`, found by name rather than by position:

- **`orderHasDelayedAirShipment`** (`routes/retail.js`) — true when a parcel has `mode = 'air'`, was dispatched, is delivered, and landed more than one day after dispatch.
- It raises three things already: the **`AIR DELAYED · contact customer`** badge in the orders list, a **"Delivery needs a call"** dashboard card, and an **`order_air_delayed`** customer notification that replaces the cheerful delivered message with a warning not to eat the perishables.
- The order drawer prints **two numbered instructions** — contact the customer, then contact the carrier for delay compensation — and offers **one button** underneath them.
- That button writes **`retail_shipments.air_delay_cleared_at` / `air_delay_cleared_by`**, and nothing else. No money, no stock, no record of which of the two instructions was actually carried out.

**So the steps are already written down. They are prose with a single checkbox under them.** This section decides that those instructions become the steps, in place. It is not a new screen and not a new module, and the detector is not replaced.

**THERE IS NO TASK OR CHECKLIST TABLE ANYWHERE IN THIS REPOSITORY.** Grepped 2026-09-11: none. A general one must not be built here. §32 already refused the mirror of this from the other side — waste is a reason, not a feature of its own — and a second way to track work is a second mechanism that then has to agree with the first one forever.

### The shape is `retail_refund_events`, deliberately

Refunds already do exactly this: one row per step (`requested | reviewing | approved | rejected | paid | withdrawn | note`) carrying an amount, a note, and whoever did it, with the status and the timestamps denormalised onto the order where a list needs them cheaply. **A delay case is the same shape and must not invent a second one.** A reader three months later wants a timeline, and the refund timeline already reads correctly.

### The four steps, and the branch

1. **Customer told** — that the parcel was late and the fresh items may not be safe. This step exists today; what changes is that it stops also meaning the other three.
2. **Claim filed with the carrier** — claim reference, amount claimed, date.
3. **Replacement sent, OR the customer refunded.** A branch, taken once. The refund half is not reimplemented: it hands to the existing refund path (`refund_status`, `retail_refund_events`).
4. **Carrier paid** — amount received, date.

### The steps live on the SHIPMENT, not on the order

An order can fan out into an air parcel and a land parcel (`retail_shipments`). Both the existing detector and the existing ack route are already scoped per parcel and per mode, and an order carrying two parcels otherwise cannot say which one was late. **Put the case on the order and that information is lost on exactly the orders that need it most.**

### What the books do — and the single row that reaches them

**THE COST OF THE FOOD IS ALREADY AN EXPENSE AND MUST NOT BE BOOKED A SECOND TIME.** Measured, because the session assumed otherwise first and was wrong: `routes/finance-summary.js` returns `cost_of_goods: null` and `gross_profit: null` with a comment saying it always will until a cost model exists, and no route in `routes/retail.js` writes an `expense_entries` row for a sale. **Food becomes an expense on the day it is bought from the supplier**, not the day it is sold. Therefore:

- **The spoiled goods the customer received — nothing is booked.** Already expensed at purchase. And it is not the tenant's loss in the first place: the carrier pays for those goods, which is Ash's own correction above.
- **The replacement goods — nothing reaches the ledger either.** Also already expensed at purchase. What must happen is that **stock goes down**, and the ¥0 order does that by the ordinary order path with nothing new invented.
- **The carrier's payment — ONE row in `income_entries`, and it is the only new entry in the books this whole case produces.**

**IT IS NOT INCOME UNTIL IT LANDS.** §87's rule for money out, restated for money in: a claim is not in the books because it was filed. A carrier that rejects the claim, or pays ¥200 against ¥300 asked, would otherwise leave money in the books that nobody ever received and nothing on screen to say so.

**The posting shape is `postClaim` in `lib/expense-posting.js`** — delete every ledger row carrying this case's id, then re-insert from the document, so the ledger always says what the document currently says and calling it twice is safe. **`income_entries` has no `claim_id`-shaped column today**; `expense_entries` has one and `income_entries` does not, so one is needed. The posted row is a projection and the Transactions screen must refuse to edit it, for the reason it already refuses a purchase-order row.

**The replacement's cost is recorded ON THE CASE, not in the ledger.** The question worth asking is whether the carrier's payment covered what it cost to put the order right, and a flat-rate carrier against a larger replacement leaves a real gap that no ledger row in this model would ever show. Recording only the money coming in makes every one of these read as free profit.

### The amounts are typed, not calculated

Carriers differ: a flat sum, a percentage, an assessed value. **A typed "claimed" and a typed "received" is correct for every tenant and every carrier with no configuration at all**, which is what Ash's "other tenants have different configuration" asks for. A rules engine that computes compensation would be considerable work and wrong for the first tenant whose carrier does it differently.

### Nothing here is carrier-specific or tenant-specific

`lib/tracking.js` already holds a general `CARRIERS` list — JD, SF, YTO, STO, ZTO, Yunda, EMS and `other` — so the claim is against whichever carrier the parcel actually carries. **No column, label or branch introduced under this section may name JD.** The existing drawer text does, and that is the text being replaced.

### Open, and deliberately not decided

- **Which parcels raise a case.** Today: `mode = 'air'` only, only once delivered, only more than one day late. A late JD land parcel and a late same-city rider parcel raise nothing at all. Ash expressed no preference when asked. It cannot be widened by simply dropping the mode test, because the threshold differs per mode — a day late is ordinary for a land parcel — so widening needs a lateness number per mode first.
- **Whether the evidence sent to the carrier is held in Tacet.** No preference expressed. The claim reference and the amounts are in scope; photographs are not, and **this phase must not make adding them harder.**
- **Which readers must exclude a ¥0 replacement order.** It must not inflate order counts or drag average order value down. The affected readers are not enumerated here and that enumeration is part of the work, not a separate question.
- **Whether a case can ever be both a replacement and a refund.** Ash chose "a refund *instead of* a replacement". Both at once was offered and not taken, so it is **not decided rather than rejected**: if a case ever needs both, that is a new ruling, not an extension of this one.

### The Chinese is not composed in this section

Per `CLAUDE.md` and `docs/tacet-delivery-vocabulary.md` Rule 4, every label this section implies takes its Chinese in the same commit as the code that uses it, declared in that document with the live candidates that were rejected. **The live pair `空运延误 · 联系客户` already exists** and the step labels should be restructured around it, or around another live pair, before anything new is minted.

### Rejected

- **Rejected: recording the spoiled goods as waste.** `waste_records` requires a `location_id` and a subject that is a material or a product **at that location**; this food is at the customer's house. It would also be the wrong claim even if the table allowed it, because the carrier pays for those goods and they are not the tenant's loss. Recorded explicitly because it is the intuitive wrong answer — a spoiled box *feels* like a loss that ought to be written down somewhere.
- **Rejected: a general task or checklist mechanism.** Stated above, and it is §32's lesson arriving from the other direction.
- **Rejected: booking the carrier's payment when the claim is filed.** §87. A rejected or part-paid claim would put money in the books that never arrived.
- **Rejected: a stock adjustment instead of a ¥0 order.** The customer needs a waybill they can follow, and in this product only an order carries a parcel. A stock adjustment has no address, no tracking number and no record of who received what.
- **Rejected: extending the existing single ack button to mean "all four steps done".** It is what exists today and it is the defect: four facts behind one checkbox cannot answer whether the carrier was ever chased.

### §98 addendum — what building it changed, and the read sites that did NOT swap (2026-09-11)

**Stages one and two are built** (the case, and the checklist that keeps it open
until the carrier answers). Stages three and four — the ¥0 replacement order and
the `income_entries` row — are not, and nothing here decides them further.

**THE THREE READ SITES DO NOT SWAP, AND THE CHANGELOG ENTRY ABOVE SAYS THEY DO.**
v4.212 states that `air_delay_cleared_at IS NULL` becomes "has an open case" in
the badge, the dashboard card and the drawer. It was written before the code and
it is wrong — recorded here rather than edited out of the entry, because a
changelog line is dated and this file does not rewrite dated claims to match what
happened next.

What was built instead: **`air_delay_cleared_at` remains the single flag meaning
"still on the worklist"**, and the case row gates who may set it. Three reasons,
in the order they decided it:

1. **It buys the weeks-long chase for nothing.** `/dashboard/ops`'s
   `delivery_alerts` already counts these orders, already ages them from
   `dispatched_at`, and already refreshes every sixty seconds. That IS the
   surface a three-week-old dispute has to sit on, and it needed no change at
   all — only the condition that takes an order off it.
2. **Swapping would have needed a backfill.** Every parcel already cleared in
   production would have to be given a closed case, or every handled order from
   the last year lights up again on the morning of the deploy.
3. **Two sources of truth for "is this finished" is the thing to avoid.** With
   the stamp kept, there is exactly one, and `lib/delay-case.js` is the only
   thing standing in front of it.

**BOTH SURFACES, ONE CHANGE, AND IT WAS NOT OPTIONAL.** The banner being replaced
was already on the phone as well as the desktop — the survey behind §98 missed
it, having grepped for the column name where `public/m.html` keys off
`o.airDelayed`. Once the server refuses the close, a phone still offering a
one-tap dismiss is §97's own "the same button with the safety removed", so the
checklist ships on both or the change is not safe to ship at all.

**WHAT IS RECORDED AS OPEN STAYS OPEN.** Air-only detection, evidence in Tacet,
which reports must skip a ¥0 order, and whether a case can be both a replacement
and a refund are all untouched by this build.

**One thing was learned that the section did not anticipate.** `none` had to
become a state that HOLDS the case open rather than one that lets it close: an
operator who never touches the dispute track has not decided not to claim, and
the two must not be the same row. Choosing not to claim is its own state and
requires a typed reason — which is what makes "the dispute with the logistics
company, **if any**" expressible at all, and it is now the thing
`scripts/test_delay_case.js` guards hardest after the refusal itself.

### §98 addendum 2 — stage four is built; stage three is NOT, and here is the measurement (2026-09-11)

**Stage four is built.** A carrier's payment posts exactly one `income_entries`
row, keyed on a new `delay_case_id`, by `lib/delay-case-posting.js` — the same
delete-then-reinsert shape `postClaim` uses, so the ledger always says what the
case currently says and calling it twice cannot bank the money twice. **Only
`paid` posts**: a filed claim posts nothing, and a rejection, a withdrawal or a
re-filing after a payment takes the row back out rather than offsetting it with a
negative one. It is the first projection this ledger has ever had on the money-IN
side; every `income_entries` row before it was hand-typed.

The row carries **no category**, deliberately. `routes/finance-transactions.js`
records that the income category list "ships empty. No defaults" so the form
cannot offer a wrong option; seeding one here to label carrier compensation would
be a library quietly deciding a question that document says is the tenant's.

### Stage three is not built, and the reason is a number

§98 recorded *which readers must exclude a ¥0 order* as open. It has now been
measured, and the answer is why the stage stopped rather than shipped.

**A ¥0 replacement order contributes ¥0 to every revenue sum, so revenue is
self-correcting and was never the problem. The problem is COUNT and AVG.** An
order that nobody paid for adds one to the order count and drags the average
order value down, on every surface that reports either.

**The gate those surfaces share is copied twelve times.**
`status IN ('paid','preparing','dispatched','delivered','awaiting_restock')` is
written out verbatim in eleven places in `routes/retail.js` and once in
`lib/finance-window.js`. **There is no single definition to amend.** And a
replacement parcel must pass through `preparing`, `dispatched` and `delivered`
to be picked, shipped and tracked — so it is inside that predicate by
construction, at all twelve. Beyond them sit the per-customer counts, which are
not gated on payment at all (`SELECT COUNT(*) FROM retail_orders WHERE
customer_id = ?` and its siblings).

**Twelve hand-copied predicates plus the ungated counts, and missing one is a
silently wrong report** — a class of defect this file exists to prevent, and one
no test currently in the tree would catch.

**What is recorded, not decided:** the safe order of work looks like
consolidating that predicate to one exported definition FIRST, as its own change
with no behaviour attached, after which excluding a replacement is one line in
one place. That is a separate PR under §36's territory, it is worth doing on its
own merits, and **it is not a decision a session may take** — it edits how every
money figure in the product is computed. Until it is taken, stage three stays
unbuilt and step three of the case remains what stages one and two shipped: an
operator's tick over a replacement they raised by hand.

### §98 addendum 3 — the paid predicate is consolidated, and stage three is now one line away (2026-09-11)

Addendum 2 recorded that the order-status allow-list every revenue figure is
gated on was written out verbatim twelve times, with no single definition to
amend, and that consolidating it was **not a decision a session may take**. Ash
took it. This records what was done, and — more usefully — what it turned out to
be.

**IT WAS NOT NEW ARCHITECTURE. IT WAS AN EXISTING DECISION BEING HONOURED.**
`lib/finance-window.js` has always said, in its own header, that it is "that
decision, taken once, for every Finance surface … **editing a constant here is
the only way to change what Finance counts**". That was true of
`routes/finance-summary.js` and `routes/finance-transactions.js`, which import
it and declare none of their own. It was quietly false of `routes/retail.js`,
which carried eleven hand-written copies of the same characters and had never
imported the module at all. The claim in that header was a description of two
files being sold as a property of the system.

**THE LIST IS NOW THE SOURCE AND THE SQL IS RENDERED FROM IT.** `PAID_STATUSES`
is the five statuses; `paidWhere(alias)` renders them, and `PAID` and `PAID_O`
are its two callers. Six of the eleven copies were alias-qualified
(`o.status IN …`) and five bare, which is why one constant could not have
replaced them and why the drift was easy to miss.

**NOTHING ABOUT WHAT IS COUNTED CHANGED**, and that is asserted rather than
asserted-in-prose: `scripts/test_paid_predicate.js` pins the generated string
byte-for-byte against a frozen copy of the pre-consolidation literal, so
reordering the list or adding a status fails a test instead of quietly
restating every money figure in the product. The same suite fails if any file
under `routes/` or `lib/` hand-writes the list again.

**FIVE NEIGHBOURING PREDICATES WERE DELIBERATELY LEFT ALONE** —
`('paid','awaiting_restock')`, `('paid','preparing')`,
`('paid','preparing','rider_pickup')` and the two channel-internal ones. They
answer different questions, folding them in would have been a behaviour change
wearing a refactor's clothes, and a test asserts they are still there.

**One existing suite had to be amended, and it argued for its own amendment.**
`scripts/test_finance_summary.js` scraped `PAID` out of the module's source with
a regex and asserted the allow-list appears exactly once. Generated output
matches neither. Both were fixed the way that file had already fixed the same
problem for `ODATE`, in a comment it wrote itself: require the module, because
that "tests the value that actually ships instead of a copy of its spelling".
The count assertion now reads zero literals and one list — the same rule, one
level further in.

**STAGE THREE IS NOW ONE LINE AWAY** and is still not built. Excluding a ¥0
replacement order is a single clause in `paidWhere`, or a sibling constant
beside it. What is still undecided is everything §98 left open about the
replacement order itself — and the per-customer counts, which are not gated on
payment at all and would need their own answer.

### §98 addendum 4 — stage three is built, and the exclusion really was one line (2026-09-11)

The ¥0 replacement order exists. §98 is complete.

**IT IS A WHOLLY ORDINARY ORDER APART FROM THE PRICE**, and that is the design.
It is created `paid` (nothing is owed, so nothing is outstanding), the warehouse
works it preparing → dispatched → delivered exactly as it works any other, stock
comes off at the preparing transition through the same
`prepareCommitUnreservedOrder` every non-reserving order already uses, and
`ensureShipments` plans its parcel so the customer gets a waybill to follow.
**Nothing on the fulfilment path is special-cased**, because a bespoke path is
one nobody maintains — and it is why the whole stage is one route, not a
subsystem.

**THE EXCLUSION WAS ONE LINE, AS PROMISED.** `paidWhere()` gained
`AND COALESCE(<alias>replacement_for_order_id, 0) = 0`, and every one of the
twelve former copies got it at once. `COALESCE` rather than `IS NULL` because
every order predating the column has NULL there and must keep counting exactly
as it always has. `scripts/test_paid_predicate.js` now runs the predicate
against a real table and asserts the figure that would have been wrong: with a
¥0 replacement counted, an average order value of 500 reads as 333.33.

**WHAT THE CUSTOMER SEES IS DELIBERATELY UNCHANGED.** Their own order list and
status buckets are not payment-gated and were not touched: they have a parcel
coming and must be able to find and track it. The exclusion is about what the
BUSINESS counts as trade, never about hiding a delivery from the person waiting
for it. The voucher-redemption counts are unaffected for a different reason — a
replacement carries no voucher.

**`remedy_cost` IS SNAPSHOT ON THE CASE, NOT DERIVED FROM THE ORDER.** The
replacement's lines are ¥0 — that is what makes it a replacement — so the order
cannot answer what putting this right cost. Only the case can, and that is the
question the case exists to answer: did the carrier's payment cover it. A later
price change must not restate a past incident, which is §32's rule for waste
applied here. An uncosted line contributes nothing rather than blocking the
replacement; the figure is a comparison aid and never a ledger entry.

**ONE REPLACEMENT PER CASE, ENFORCED.** A double-tap would otherwise send the
goods twice, and the second parcel is real stock leaving the building.

### Three existing guards caught this change, and all three were right

Recorded because the useful part is what they caught, not that they went green
afterwards.

1. **`test_customer_currency`** — the confirm text said "a ¥0 order". This
   product is multi-currency and that suite exists because a merchant trading in
   dollars once had their GMV printed in yuan. The wording now names no currency
   at all ("a no-charge order"), and the three figures the case renders go
   through `money(CUR, n)` / `ordMoney(n)`. **It also caught two ¥ literals from
   stages one and two**, live since this evening, which had evaded the check
   only because `'¥' + Number(x)` puts a quote between the symbol and the digit.
2. **`test_finance_summary`** — its fixture built `retail_orders` without the new
   column and `PAID` now reads it. The fixture names its columns explicitly now,
   so the next column does not break it.
3. **`test_handle_threading_batch2`** — pins the number of `ensureShipments` call
